subtopic: THE CROWN PRINCE OF JAPAN

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PRESENCE OF DISTINGUISHED VISITOR IN GALLERY
subtopic: THE CROWN PRINCE OF JAPAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think all hon. members would wish me to mention at this time that we are honoured today by the presence in the diplomatic gallery of His Imperial Highness the Crown Prince of Japan. I am sure we are all unanimous in wishing to extend to him a most warm welcome on this occasion. His Imperial Highness is visiting Canada on his way' to London to attend the coronation of our own beloved sovereign Queen Elizabeth. The devoted affection we all have for our own sovereign makes it quite easy for us to understand the high regard in which his illustrious father and the imperial family are held by the people of Japan.
His Imperial Majesty the Emperor of Japan is a symbol of his state, and of course the history of the relations between Japan and the western world was darkened by heavy shadows during the tragic years of war. But that is now something of the past. I think that the presence here of His Imperial Highness the Crown Prince, and the important mission on which he is engaged at this time, is a happy confirmation of the fact that those tragic years were of short duration and were, in fact, repugnant to the intimate feelings of all the peoples of the nations who were engaged in war during those tragic years. This mission of His Imperial Highness is a happy omen of better relations between our peoples, and of a more effective and keener desire in all our countries to work together for the welfare of the whole free human race.
We are most happy to welcome His Royal Highness and to say to him that we hope he is enjoying, and will enjoy, his visit throughout Canada, and that he will take back to his country the knowledge that there is a genuine good will towards his country in this land of ours which, like his own, borders on this great highway of the Pacific ocean which has been, and will continue to
be, a highway for the maintenance of political, economic and trade relationships that will be mutually beneficial to our two peoples.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
maintopic: PRESENCE OF DISTINGUISHED VISITOR IN GALLERY
subtopic: THE CROWN PRINCE OF JAPAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to join with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in extending a hearty welcome to the Crown Prince of Japan who in himself here today expresses the similarity between our own monarchical system and that which he represents. As the Prime Minister has already said, the relationship between our respective nations has had its unhappy period. It would also be well to remember that we had an earlier period of alliance in which our relationship was warm and friendly. It is part of the genius of our free system, which is now represented in the parliamentary system of Japan as well as that of Canada, that out of conflict we seek friendship in the years afterwards.
I would hope that the visit on this occasion of His Imperial Highness to this country may emphasize in the minds of the people of his own nation as well as of ours that, with the lessons of the tragic years still clearly in our minds, we are seeking to build stronger understandings of the value of freedom.
We recognize the great achievements of a nation which has reached a proud position in the world as a producer of goods of high quality. We recognize the industry of the people of Japan. We recognize their loyalty to their own traditions. In extending this welcome today to His Imperial Highness, who is part of the system of democratic monarchy which has been established in Japan, we earnestly hope that during the future these nations may come closer together in striving for great achievements along the paths of peace.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STEAM AND MOTOR ENGINEER CERTIFICATES, RADIOTELEGRAPH INSTALLATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: This bill was amended rather extensively in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I wonder whether the parliamentary assistant is going to give any explanation of these amendments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STEAM AND MOTOR ENGINEER CERTIFICATES, RADIOTELEGRAPH INSTALLATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
The amendments, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra says, are somewhat extensive. They appear in Votes

and Proceedings of March 31, but there is no controversy, as I understand it, in connection with the clause that is now before us.
The committee heard representatives and counsel of the shipping industry, and in particular the British Columbia Tug Boat Association, the British Columbia Coastwise Operators' Association, counsel and representatives of the Dominion Marine Association and some of the individual shipping companies.
The major amendments that were made in committee had to do with radiotelephone equipment. As the bill was originally drafted, it was suggested that radiotelegraph should be compulsory in vessels of the sizes described in the bill. In committee the officials of the Department of Transport indicated that, provided there was adequate radiotelephone equipment, it was their intention to provide exemptions from the telegraph requirements up to certain limits and in certain waters if radiotelephone was carried. The industry made representations that practically all vessels of the size we were concerned with, particularly on the west coast plying in coastal waters, were now equipped with radiotelephone equipment. It was therefore suggested that although radiotelephone equipment up to now had been provided by them on a voluntary basis, instead of requiring them to come and seek exemptions for this large number of vessels we should make radiotelephone equipment mandatory, and then have a higher tonnage limit for the requirement of radiotelegraphy. That I think in essence is the nature of the amendments that were made in committee. The amendments were made after legal and other officers of the Department of Transport consulted with counsel for the shipping companies, and I think that, with the exception of the continuing insistence upon the original radiotelegraph stipulations in the bill in respect of passenger vessels, counsel for the shipping industry and all members of the committee were satisfied with the amendments made.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STEAM AND MOTOR ENGINEER CERTIFICATES, RADIOTELEGRAPH INSTALLATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I could not hear everything the parliamentary assistant said, but I gathered he went a little far in his statements concerning the use of the radiotelephone. As the bill was originally drawn it provided for the installation of wireless equipment, and extended that requirement right down to the tugs on the west coast used to tow booms of logs.
When the committee sat, representatives of the west coast tow-boat industry protested a provision under which they would have to carry on their tugs wireless operators and wireless equipment. I believe they had a
Canada Shipping Act
just ground for complaint on that score. As the parliamentary assistant knows, in the final analysis their tugs were exempted from such provision and, instead, were placed under the provision covering ships on the great lakes and the upper St. Lawrence, in respect of which the primary requirement is the provision of the radiotelephone as distinct from the wireless.
I would not want the impression to get abroad however that the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act have eased up the requirements on passenger vessels to carry wireless operators and equipment. For some time there has been a campaign on the part of ship owners to have the wireless replaced by radiotelephone, the latter being operated by one or other of the ship's officers. There has also been a tendency on our coast to have the wireless operators carry on other work. For example, they might act as pursers or as freight checkers, or in some other capacities.
There is no doubt it was the desire of the shipping companies to reduce so far as possible the number of passenger ships on which wireless operators would have to be carried. As the act will stand when these amendments go through, the primary requirement for a passenger vessel will be the carrying of a wireless operator, and exemptions will be granted only at the discretion of the Department of Transport.
I believe that is the way the law should stand-in other words that wireless operators should be carried unless the Department of Transport sees fit to exempt any vessel, or to exempt certain trips. I hope the department will be most careful in granting such exemptions. Let the officials of the department remember that, in the final analysis, if lives are lost on either of our coasts because of a relaxing of regulations, the responsibility will rest squarely with the department.
We have heard the suggestion, for example, that it should not be necessary to carry wireless operators on passenger vessels plying between Vancouver and Victoria. Some of those ships carry as many as two thousand passengers; and while the radiotelephone may be ample protection in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, there may very well come the hundredth case when, because of there being no wireless operator on a vessel, a good many hundred lives might be lost.
Because of the international convention it is necessary for those ships to carry wireless operators between Vancouver or Victoria and Seattle. But it is suggested that, while they

Canada Shipping Act
have to do that, perhaps the shipping companies could be freed from the obligation of carrying wireless operators between Vancouver and Victoria. I do not believe the department should make any such exemption.
There is the further suggestion that there need not be wireless operators on passenger vessels, so long as they are in the waters between Vancouver island and the mainland. It is admitted that once a ship gets beyond the northern tip of Vancouver island wireless operators should be required. The companies are suggesting however that they should not have to carry such operators between Vancouver and the northern tip of Vancouver island. Let me remind the committee that Hippie rock lies in that inside passage between Vancouver island and the mainland, and that it represents one of the greatest marine hazards on the west coast. I am afraid that some day there will be a terrible wreck because of that rock. In any event there should be no relaxation such as has been suggested. Wireless operators should be required on that trip up to the northern end of Vancouver island just as they are required in the waters lying to the north of the island.
I would point out that last summer there was a very serious wreck on our coast when the Princess Kathleen ran aground and was lost. Fortunately no lives were lost; but the vessel, the flagship of the Canadian Pacific Railway fleet, was a total loss. I understand that at the time of the accident the radiotelephone was of no use. I am told by responsible men that the radiotelephone on the Princess Kathleen was not able to do the job it was expected to do. Apparently nothing was sent out over the wireless because of orders to that effect by the captain.
Certainly the radiotelephone is a great help; but the time has not yet come when it can be relied upon exclusively and the wireless dispensed with or the wireless operator given other work to do. Let me point out again that responsibility for any undue relaxation in the terms of the Canada Shipping Act will rest with the Department of Transport, and I would hope that the department would, be most careful in granting exemptions.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STEAM AND MOTOR ENGINEER CERTIFICATES, RADIOTELEGRAPH INSTALLATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I could not
hear all of the explanation made by the parliamentary assistant. However, it is my understanding that certain modifications or amendments have been made in the bill as it was before it went to the committee. He said also that these changes or modifications were acceptable to the owners and I believe to the officers of the Department of Transport.

In that connection may I ask if representatives of the personnel on the ships appeared before the committee, and did they agree to these modifications? This matter has been discussed by the personnel and crews of ships and sailing vessels for a long long time. I have had much correspondence from and many interviews with representatives of those who sail the ships. They are the people who are concerned because they are the ones most likely to lose their lives in case of accident.
I can well understand that the owners would approach this question, not with the idea of saving lives but with the idea of saving dollars. They could very well agree with the modifications, but are those modifications acceptable to the crews who sail these vessels and who are likely to lose their lives in case of accident at sea? I think we have been most backward in enacting safety measures and certainly the time has arrived when we should make them the best possible.
I should like to refer also to the matter mentioned by the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra, that is that the personnel in charge of radiotelegraph and radiotelephone equipment should be full-time employees and should not be asked to carry out any other work. Unless they are full-time employees the possibility is that they may not be on hand to receive a particular message and certainly would not be there at all times to see that the equipment was kept in proper condition so that it functioned at all times.
I am apprehensive of the effects of these modifications. I imagine that all I can do at this stage is to express the hope that the Department of Transport will be most careful about granting exemptions in this matter. We have had some serious marine accidents in different parts of this country during the last few years. When regulations were proposed by the Department of Transport in an effort to prevent such accidents in the future I supported the Minister of Transport as strongly as I could. I felt that if we are going to put the onus on the minister to provide safety regulations at sea he should be supported in doing that by members of this house. I do hope that the lives of the crews on these ships and the lives of the passengers who may be involved were taken into consideration, as well as the cost of the installations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STEAM AND MOTOR ENGINEER CERTIFICATES, RADIOTELEGRAPH INSTALLATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Probably I should reply at this point to the hon. member for Vancouver East and assure him that while there have been some modifications of the proposed amendments in the committee, actually the

till as it comes before us from the committee is a considerable advance over the present law. There has been no relaxation in the case of passenger vessels from the intent in the bill as drafted originally. The evidence given in the committee was that most cargo vessels of over 500 tons were voluntarily carrying radiotelephone equipment. This bill makes it mandatory so that these safety measures are considerably advanced from the law as it has been up to mow.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STEAM AND MOTOR ENGINEER CERTIFICATES, RADIOTELEGRAPH INSTALLATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few minutes to deal with one or two matters which are of great interest to those who sail the waters of the bay of Fundy. There would seem to be some difference of opinion between members *on the east coast and on the west coast with regard to the value of radiotelephones. I think I can say without any fear of contradiction that on the Atlantic coast and in the bay of Fundy area the radiotelephone is considered to be one of the greatest advantages that the fishermen, the boatmen, and all those who go down to the sea in ships have ever had in so far as the protection of their ships is concerned.
To the best of my knowledge and belief there are only two steamships plying the waters of the bay of Fundy, one being the Princess Helene, which plies between Saint John and Digby and-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STEAM AND MOTOR ENGINEER CERTIFICATES, RADIOTELEGRAPH INSTALLATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Two passenger steamships?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STEAM AND MOTOR ENGINEER CERTIFICATES, RADIOTELEGRAPH INSTALLATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: -the Grand Manan III, which plies between Grand Manan and Saint John. Of necessity these ships are furnished with telegraphic equipment, but if anything should happen to one of these ships there would be only one other ship in the area which could pick up the message. If anything happened to the Grand Manan III, the only ship in the bay of Fundy that would by able to pick up the message would be the Princess Helene, and vice versa.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STEAM AND MOTOR ENGINEER CERTIFICATES, RADIOTELEGRAPH INSTALLATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Or a large cargo vessel.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STEAM AND MOTOR ENGINEER CERTIFICATES, RADIOTELEGRAPH INSTALLATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
There are no large cargo vessels in that area. I would point out that 90 per cent of the boats that ply these waters are equipped with radiotelephones. Another great advantage in the use of this type of equipment is that anyone can operate a radiotelephone whereas it takes a trained operator to operate the telegraphic equipment. For that reason I would submit that radiotelephone equipment is necessary in the bay of Fundy area. I would think that the installation of telegraphic equipment in the boats I have mentioned would be a step
Canada Shipping Act
backward rather than a step forward. There would be much more protection afforded by the use of radiotelephones because of the greater number of boats that could pick up a message. It would take an enormous amount of the responsibility off the shoulders of thflse who operate these boats if they knew that they could get in touch with their home offices or with other boats.
I would suggest also that criticism with regard to the equipment on passenger boats is always justified. I feel that these boats should have every type of equipment necessary for their proper protection. I do not want to give the impression that I am opposed to that, because I believe it is right. As has been pointed out by hon. members who have spoken previously, there have been a number of marine disasters in this country in the last few years, which fact clearly indicates that perhaps we should be more severe in enforcing the regulations.
There is one other matter I should like to bring to the attention of the parliamentary assistant. There seems to be some misunderstanding between the customs officials in some of the ports in Saint John and Charlotte counties and the officials of the Department of Justice. When this bill was in committee I was given to understand that no effort would be made to force small cargo boats to comply with all these regulations. The particular type of boat I have in mind is one on which there would be a master or skipper or captain and an engineer. These men realize the dangers that may be encountered and they have made provision for their own safety.
Recently a boat from Grand Manan island, whose skipper I know very well, came into Saint John, but when the captain went to get his clearance papers to return to Grand Manan he was told by the customs that they were unable to give them to him until he had got in touch with the steamboat inspector. As I said before, I believe that there is a very definite place for steamboat inspection, but I cannot think of any argument in favour of enforcing steamboat inspection in connection with fishing craft and small cargo boats that do not carry passengers. I would ask the parliamentary assistant and the officials of the department to give this matter their serious thought.
I have received a number of letters and telegrams about this matter, and I sent the minister a copy of one particular letter. So far as the equipment on his boat is concerned, he had fire extinguishers, he had a dory, which is considered to be a lifeboat, and he had covers for the dory to keep out

the winter weather. He had all the equipment that was necessary. When the inspector looked over the boat he suggested that he should have rails and wire cables tor his protection. In the particular type of work that this man carries on it would be utterly impossible to have rails on the bdtit. It would be helpful in some cases but in the sardine industry it would be impossible to have rails and guards of the type that would satisfy the steamboat inspection service.
I ask the parliamentary assistant to go into this matter very carefully because I feel it would impose a hardship upon these men, who are finding it difficult to get along at this time. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STEAM AND MOTOR ENGINEER CERTIFICATES, RADIOTELEGRAPH INSTALLATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
It is a pleasure to hear a seaman like the hon. member for Charlotte get up and take part in the discussion of the bill. I am also an old-time sailor. I admire the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra greatly as a lawyer and for his common sense. I also admire the hon. member for Vancouver East, whose judgment I am sure is very good in a great many matters; but I think he went a little too far this morning when he suggested that the operators of steamboats were more concerned with the saving of dollars than the saving of lives. I am sure he meant it to be a fair comment but I think he would not care to repeat it after giving the matter due consideration. I do not think it is generally known that the whole concept of safety at sea has changed completely in the last ten years, as the hon. member for Charlotte said, with the installation of radiotelephones on hundreds and hundreds of vessels plying the waters on the Pacific coast. A new era has come into being so far as safety of life at sea is concerned.
I should like to offer to the parliamentary assistant another comment which I hope will be of value to his department. I must say that these amendments to the Canada Shipping Act were brought in with very little notice to the shipping industry on the Pacific coast. As a matter of fact there was almost a panic in the industry when those engaged in it finally learned what the contents of the bill were after it had been printed. When a bill of this kind is introduced in 

the other place and is passed by the gentlemen there it carries with it a certain stamp of approval, and one naturally considers that a body of that kind would give such a bill very mature consideration. But we find that it went through the other place with a minimum of discussion and examination and then came to the House of Commons. As hon. members who were on the committee all know, very substantial changes had to be made in the bill because as first presented to us it was ridiculous so far as the west coast industry is concerned. In making these comments, I do not wish to cast any reflection on the Department of Transport, but I hope they will make the gentlemen in the other place feel that when legislation is presented to them for the first time _ they should give it very careful examination before according it their stamp of approval.

Passenger vessels. Unless
there has been a change fairly recently, the situation is that the purser on the ship operates the wireless telegraphy system. I am thinking of voyages in particular between the mainland and Newfoundland, from North Sydney to Port aux Basques. The purser on that run takes care of the passengers and he has to take care of the manifests. In doing all that work he is a very busy man, and the result is that for quite a long time he is not able to be in the wireless room while the ship is actually en route. There are two factors with respect to that situation. The purser is not only seriously overworked, but I submit there is also a danger to the ship itself and possibly a danger to other ships that may be imperilled and cannot reach this particular ship for assistance.

1 understand that there is a radar system on the ship, and although I am not certain I believe it is also operated by the purser. If he is not there to oversee the radar system, it is not of very much avail. I think that is correct but my information is not of recent date. The last time I remember discussing the matter was about a year and a half ago, and the situation then was as I have described it today. If that is the case today- and I presume it is-I suggest that there should be a separate wireless operator for the ship independent of the purser, and I am not certain that that should not apply to all Canadian National ships in the Newfoundland service. It may not be required on some voyages, but there are a number of long voyages running from St. John's to Labrador in the coastal route, and the purser is an extremely busy man at times. I submit that provision should be made to include the particular type of ships now used by Canadian National in the Newfoundland service.

He has talked about getting the comments of those who are most competent to judge this matter. If he will discuss it with his fishermen friends as I have discussed it with mine and also with
Canada Shipping Act
his sailor friends, he will find that so far as safety of life at sea is concerned the radiotelephone has made by far the greatest contribution to the welfare of those concerned and, incidentally, to their domestic happiness. I know that has only happened in the fishing industry in recent years. I might tell him that pilots going aboard ships not equipped with radiotelephones very often take a walkie-talkie telephone aboard so that they can make full use of the radar equipment on the ships. In many cases they found it much easier to get into the harbour of Vancouver if they were allowed to talk with the operator on the bridge concerning the traffic which might be coming through. So far as the member for Vancouver East is concerned, I ask him to please give me credit for perhaps not always looking at things from an economic angle. There is one point I should like to make. I do not think anyone is questioning the value of radiotelephone. I realize it is used very extensively on the west coast, and it will be used on passenger vessels regardless of whether or not they are required by law to use it. The point I am trying to make, and I think the member for Vancouver East is also, is that we do not want the law which requires a wireless installation and a wireless operator interfered with. We are demanding that the Department of Transport see to it that this equipment, which is designed for saving lives, should not be discarded in favour of the radiotelephone; that is as far as it goes.

Indian Act

The way the bill is drawn now, I think it will not be interfered with, provided the Department of Transport does not start issuing exemptions indiscriminately.

The house resumed, from Monday, April 13, consideration in committee of Bill No. 37, to amend the Indian Act-Mr. Harris-Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

On section 1-Loans to Indians.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS, SEIZURE OF GOODS, ETC.
speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement in connection with this bill?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS, SEIZURE OF GOODS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the amendments are quite simple and can be explained very briefly. Section 1 has to do with adding to the powers of the department the power to grant loans to Indians for the clearing of lands, an authority which the department does not have at the moment and thinks we should have in order to encourage the Indians to break up the lands and put them into production.
Section 2 has to do with adding a section number, that is 92, to the section which gives authority to seize goods which are illegally taken from the reserve. This was a typographical error on our part in not having this section mentioned in the bill which went through the house two years ago.
Section 3 has to do with another legal difficulty. I think I explained to the committee when we amended the bill two years ago that, in some cases, we had found that orders in council had not been passed by the governor in council as required according to a decision of the supreme court at that time, validating the surrender and sale of land. The amendments in the bill at that time provided for the conditions which are now in subsection (a) of section 124. At the time we overlooked the fact that there were still some sales of land which had been made some time before but which were only evidenced by agreements for sale, that is the money had not yet been fully paid, and when the letters patent would be granted eventually they would not be covered by subsection (a). Subsection (b) is, therefore, added in order to validate these sales which may take effect from time to time when the final payments are made and the letters patent granted.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS, SEIZURE OF GOODS, ETC.
speechtext:
So far as any improvement in the welfare of the Indians is concerned, I think the first of these clauses is the most important. I am very glad that loans will now be available to the Indians for breaking up the land. As a matter of fact, I should like to see the department handling loans to Indians for farm purposes undertake a more vigorous program which would enable the Indians to make a better livelihood. So far as I can make out, that has not been done in the past.
I am informed that a large number of Indians have had difficulty in getting loans for the purpose of buying machinery and other things which would enable them to

carry on farm operations more efficiently and thus make a better living. I would ask the minister at this time how many loans are now in effect under this particular section of the Indian Act, that is for agriculture and other allied purposes.

position to give that information. I had expected to do that on my estimates. My recollection of the figures is that not much more than half of the amount voted was in use. I explained to the officials of the Indian affairs branch that parliament intended that money to be used if the circumstances were at all justifiable and that if the security looked to be reasonable they need not necessarily look for the last ounce of security in order to aid an Indian. Since that time there has been a liberalization of the terms on which loans are made. However, if my hon. friend would not mind, I would prefer to give the details on my estimates.

speechtext: In extending loans to the Indians, I wonder whether the minister would consider the encouragement of the credit union as a vehicle for carrying on this work? I notice a steady progress among the Indians in my part of the country, as a result of the great attention being paid to them by the minister and the officers of his department. In many cases we find them becoming quite self-supporting in agriculture in engaging in the cattle industry and the operation of saw mills and in the shipping of produce. There is at Pemberton in the adjoining riding a co-operative which is composed largely of Indians who grade and ship seed potatoes and do so very profitably. As I say, I know of groups of them working in the saw mill together successfully, manufacturing and delivering lumber and sharing the profit in the usual way. The way they could be encouraged would be to set up credit unions throughout the country where large sections of the population are Indian. They have a strong sense of responsibility. I think that it would be a step forward to initiate these credit unions and to encourage them to do their own banking and their own borrowing-always, of course, with the support and encouragement of the department.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, others have called me an Indian, but I now have just cause to be called one. The reason I rise at this time is this. speechtext: Will the minister tell us whether this amendment, which is indicated at the end of the clause at the bottom of the page, extends to permitting one of his officers mentioned in the section to make this search without a warrant? That is something which would be important, I think, particularly in so far as the right to make this search off the reserve is concerned. I think we need to give fairly sweeping powers to the peace officers in order to protect the Indians, but I just wonder whether we should go so far-as it, seems to me this goes-as to give the right to enter and search on suspicion without a warrant off a reserve.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS, SEIZURE OF GOODS, ETC.
speechtext: When the act was drafted three years ago, as my hon. friend knows, we discussed this particular section. It is clear that the superintendent and the peace officer should have all the authority which would be applicable in the case of an ordinary police officer. We also said at the time we hoped that it would not be necessary to authorize this authority off the reserve, since the ordinary police facilities would be available there, and that presumably there would be cases where the superintendent might conceivably follow a motorcar and the like, which was creating this offence, and might perhaps overtake it outside the reserve; that with these exceptions it would be expected that we would use the ordinary police facilities where they are available.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS, SEIZURE OF GOODS, ETC.
speechtext:
I was going to raise the point that was raised by the hon. member for Kamloops. I am still a bit concerned about this section. It is proposed that any peace officer or a superintendent, or any person authorized by the minister, may enter, open and search any place or thing in or upon which he reasonably believes any such goods or chattels may be found. I have no objection to this authority being extended to the peace officer or the superintendent, but I am surprised that this authority should be extended to any person designated by the minister and to be exercised apparently anywhere. As far as the reservation itself is concerned, I have no objection to any officer of the department, we will say, employed upon that reservation doing whatever is necessary upon the reservation in order to

protect the Indians; but when you authorize any person whom the minister may designate to go into any place off that reservation and make a search, then I for one believe we are going too far. I have enough confidence in the peace officer and the superintendent to think that they can do the job without extending that further authority under this act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS, SEIZURE OF GOODS, ETC.
speechtext: Our difficulty is that there may not be a superintendent. Superintendents go on vacation and they are ill. Sometimes they are out of office, retired and may be out some time before another is appointed in their places. This is intended to cover an instance of that kind. I have no desire and no intention of appointing anyone who is not familiar with the work that he is bound to do. It is only to cover the cases where you have not a person designated under the section but who is performing the functions of that person that you can designate another person.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS, SEIZURE OF GOODS, ETC.
speechtext: It is a fact that a peace officer is always available. The R.C.M.P. have jurisdiction on the reservation and off. It occurs to me that while the superintendent himself may be away, some person upon the reservation, some authority associated with his department, would probably have the power to carry on in place of the superintendent on this kind of thing in places off the reservation. It occurs to me there will always be an officer of the R.C.M.P. available to conduct that search off the reservation. I for one am not satisfied that the power should be given to a person designated by the minister.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS, SEIZURE OF GOODS, ETC.
speechtext: Let me add one word. As my hon. friend knows, the R.C.M.P. are often called to give some evidence in court and the like, and while I admit it is probably making a rather fine point, nevertheless we do believe that there are occasions when all the officers designated here will not be available. It is only in that case that we want to designate some other person, and it would be someone familiar with our work, and presumably a person in our employment, if at all possible, who would be clothed with this rather extraordinary power, which I am sure is not used very often in any event.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS, SEIZURE OF GOODS, ETC.
speechtext: Would the minister consider meeting the point by writing in a few words? It seems to me it could be met by adding after the word "minister" in line 18 the words: "when a peace officer or superintendent is not available".

I have no objection to doing that, Mr. Chairman, if my hon. friend realizes the difficulty we are trying to overcome. We are trying to overcome the difficulty of making a seizure of goods being taken
Indian Act
illegally from the reserve. You must have persons available to take that action as quickly as possible. Therefore he is imposing upon me the obligation, or rather upon the department, the necessity of sending a wire to the minister from some remote part advising me that neither of these persons is available, and asking me to designate another person. And presumably after that time we may or may not be able to recover the goods.
I would ordinarily follow this practice, anyway. The superintendent and the R.C.M.P. are clothed with the authority under the section. speakeroldname: Mr. W. M. Benidickson (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFINITIONS, REMOVING LICENCE FEE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should make a few remarks on second reading of the bill. The main purpose of course is to implement government policy as announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his budget speech with respect to the elimination of the licence fee for private radio receiving stations.
The Minister of Finance stated that the order in council setting the present licence fee of $2.50 would be revoked, effective from April 1. The Radio Act, under which this licence has been levied in the past, requires that all private receiving sets used for the reception of broadcasting must be licensed. So that if the licence fee is abolished it follows that there is need for an amending act.
Where radio receiving equipment is operated for commercial gain, such as commercial

subscription radio receiving systems where sound or television programs are received by a centralized apparatus and retransmitted to different receiving sets on a charge basis, it is considered that the operation of this type of station should be controlled and licensed. Provision therefore is made in the bill for licensing broadcasting receiving stations operated commercially for gain, with the licence fee to be fixed by the governor in council.
Provision is also made in the bill for the transfer to the Radio Act of a section that for some time has been in the Canadian Broadcasting Act, and was section 23 of that act. This section authorized the governor in council to make regulations prohibiting or regulating the use of any machinery, apparatus or equipment causing or liable to cause interference with radio reception. The house will recall that in 1951 section 23 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act containing these provisions was repealed, as it was recognized that the proper place for this provision was in the Radio Act.
However, it was provided that the repeal of the section would not come into force until proclaimed; and it has not been proclaimed until now because, until this time, it was not possible to transfer it to the Radio Act. Thus the amendment to the Radio Act covering the transfer of section 23. The scope of the section has been enlarged slightly to cover the sale as well as the use of any machinery, apparatus or equipment causing or liable to cause interference with radio reception.
There are regulations now in force which were made in 1941, under section 23 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act, for the purpose . of controlling radio interference, and these regulations will be continued in force under the Radio Act.
The other amendments in the bill delete the references to private receiving stations where these references are no longer required in the act, by reason of the elimination of the licence fee for private receiving stations.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFINITIONS, REMOVING LICENCE FEE, ETC.

Mr. Speaker, this bill seems to be one which merits support, particularly that part of it which does away with the necessity for the payment of a radio licence fee by all those people in the country who have radio sets.
As the parliamentary assistant knows, the Progressive Conservative party for many years has been advocating that this licence fee should be abolished, and we are glad to
Radio Act

Mr. Speaker, I have no prepared statement as to the purposes of the bill other than the general one that it amends the citizenship act in a number of instances. With respect to the discussion in the other place, my recollection is that there was an attempt to amend the bill in one particular which failed in committee and was not then pursued in the other proceedings of the other place. With respect to that particular point,
I can assure my hon. friend that I propose to have the relevant section stand for the course of the next hour and a half, and it is possible that we may suggest some alternative when it is reached. Therefore my hon. friend can be assured on that score that further consideration will be given.
Generally speaking, the amendments to the act extend to persons not now covered by the citizenship act the right to be Canadian citizens. Furthermore, in the case of persons who lost that citizenship on the first of January, 1947, by reason of being naturalized Canadian citizens who were living abroad for a period of six years and who had not registered and thereby retained their right of citizenship, we have extended that period of six years for another four years, so that they may continue to have the opportunity of registering and retaining their citizenship in that way.
There are other provisions consequent upon the Immigration Act, which I hope is going to be proclaimed soon, so that the definition of domicile will be in conformity with that act. There are other provisions extending the authority of the governor in council to name persons and courts who may do the work of citizenship under the act. I think I can show


that is necessary in order to make it more convenient for persons to become Canadian citizens than is the case at the moment. Generally, the amendments are as the result of five years' experience, and I think they are more liberal than anything we have had up to the present time. While it is the desire of the government that citizenship should not be taken lightly nor obtained lightly, nevertheless the experience we have had indicates that the act when first passed did not contemplate all the possible combinations of circumstances that existed under the old naturalization act, and as time goes on we desire to clear these up so that persons who have the right to be Canadians will have the legal right under the act and not by administrative process.

speechtext:
This is quite a lengthy and complicated section. Indeed, the whole act is quite complicated, and the amendments seem to be quite technical. I am particularly concerned about subsection 2 of what will be section 4 in the act. It seems to me that under paragraph (b) there is room for the possibility of abuse. It seems to me that it makes it possible for a person who has lived outside of Canada for any length of time you may care to mention, say 10 years or more, without any intention of retaining his Canadian citizenship, suddenly finding that for some reason or other it was advantageous for him to do so, to try to get it back. He then files a declaration of retention and gets a certificate of Canadian citizenship, even although he may, in the meantime, have abandoned his intention of retaining Canadian citizenship.
I think there should be something in that section requiring a person, under those circumstances, to make some affirmative proof that he had never abandoned the intention of retaining Canadian citizenship. Otherwise, it seems to me it would open up the possibility that he may, after 10 or 15 years abroad without having the actual intention of retaining Canadian citizenship, find it advantageous, for some real or fancied reason, to file his application, and he may in fact get back his Canadian citizenship.

I quite agree that we ought to take precautions against any person under those circumstances, but I think the hon. member has not quite appreciated the class of person to which this subsection applies. This only applies to the person who is born abroad of Canadian parents and who, by all citizenship acts, has the right to elect which nationality he may have when he reaches 21. This amendment alters the existing law only to the extent that, instead of forcing him to make the election within one year after reaching 21, he would have three years. In a number of cases we have had some difficulty with people who say, "We did not know that was the law." We have to realize that the act is still only six years old and a good many people, including Canadians born abroad of Canadian parents, are still finding out their rights. We ought to be a little generous towards them. There is no possibility that anyone could wait for a period longer than three years after his 21st birthday to exercise this right.

We expect to do that under certain conditions in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, although that may not be necessary now that there are additional judges there.
Northern Quebec is another instance where there may not be courts to handle these cases. We would like to have the power to designate someone in lieu of a court where a court is not available to hear the application within a reasonable time. This is not entirely academic as there have been cases where a judge has died and because of delay in appointing his successor it has been impossible to have these hearings held within a reasonable time after the application is made. There is no intention whatever of taking away from any existing court any of its present privileges and powers. The only desire is to supplement them should it be necessary in the interests of granting citizenship reasonably soon after the application is made.
I quite agree with my hon. friend about the solemnity of the occasion. Since I became minister we have done our best to make the granting of naturalization a solemn occasion. As I said in my opening remarks, we do not want to have a uniform ceremony, we want to leave to the judge a little bit of individuality and expression. But we would hope that they would impress upon the applicant, and upon themselves and the court officials, the fact that this was something that should be remembered by the applicant until he died. He could make the ceremonies simple and perhaps even short if court work required it, but nevertheless solemn and impressive. We would not appoint anyone who would not carry out these particular objectives.

"Clerk'' or "clerk of the court" Includes all officers exercising the functions of prothonotary, registrar or clerk of any court having jurisdiction under this act,-


That, of course, refers to the courts as they are set up at the present time.
-and, where a person is designated by the governor in council to act as a court for the purposes of this act, means any such officer approved by the minister and available to assist the said person as his clerk or, if no such officer is so approved, means the said person.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS

speakeroldname: Hon. Hugues Lapointe (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved
subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext: the second reading of Bill 336, to provide assistance for the higher education of children of certain deceased members of the armed forces and of other persons.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext: Is the minister going to give an explanation?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned the other day on the resolution, the purpose of this bill is to provide financial assistance for the children of veterans who died as a result of military service during world war I, world war II or in Korea. It is intended to assist children who are pensioned under the Pension Act to obtain an education above the level of high school matriculation.
The bill provides for the payment of university fees and a monthly allowance while in attendance at a university for a period of four years. As I mentioned the other day, there are approximately 12,000 children receiving pension under schedule B of the Pension Act, all of whom would be potential university students. Under this legislation, when a child has graduated from high school he will be in position to obtain assistance for his higher education, or vocational training of the type that calls for high school matriculation such as teachers' college, provincial normal schools or nursing schools at Canadian universities.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the resolution was before the house the other day we had an explanation from the minister, and a number of hon. members spoke. Since I have received the bill and read it I have been greatly disappointed, and I am satisfied that that will be the general feeling. There was general approval in the press and among all concerned when it was intimated that something would be done toward assisting the children of war veterans who had been killed overseas to obtain a higher education.
Since the war ended it has been generally realized that the children of deceased war veterans should receive special consideration as far as education is concerned because they had a special claim on the public of Canada. It was hoped that a bill of this kind would have been brought in long ago. Everyone

Armed Forces
realized that the widow of a soldier who had been killed overseas would not be in position with her limited means to provide this type of education for her children. Like everything else, the cost of education has increased greatly, and it was realized by the war veterans committee as far back as 1946 when we were considering the veterans charter that this matter should be considered. It has been brought up practically every year, either in the house, by the Legion or by some other veterans' organization. As I said a moment ago, there were great expectations as far as this bill was concerned.
The bill certainly does not go as far as we had been led to believe it would. My opinion was that the children of deceased war veterans were to be given the same educational opportunities as the veterans themselves were given on their return from overseas. I should like to read the recommendation of the Canadian Legion submitted to the government on November 12, 1952, which was as follows:
Recommendation-in respect of children of deceased service men
That the federal government instigate a policy for the children of deceased service men similar to that in force for single student veterans attending university or vocational training schools and receiving a monthly allowance under the rehabilitation act.
They recommended the adoption of a policy similar to that which had been adopted in connection with single student veterans. Anyone who is familiar with the veterans charter and who considers what is intended to be done under this bill for the children of deceased war veterans will realize that there is no comparison at all. As a matter of fact, I think in this bill the government is being very niggardly. It is not permitted to refer to the different sections, but the bill does mention what the government intends to pay and the amount is very small when compared with what is necessary to provide an education.
When we consider the cost of living, when we consider the cost of room and board, of clothes, of books, of travelling, of all these necessary things, and then consider the small monthly pittance provided under this bill we cannot help but realize how inadequate it is. I would point out that the children concerned are comparatively young, 16, 17 and 18 years of age; they are not to toe compared to the men who came back from overseas. During the four months of vacation these mature men can earn a good deal of money, but young people of 15, 16, 17 or 18 years of age, many of whom will be attending university, will have very little

opportunity to earn money to assist in obtaining their education.
There is another matter I wish to bring up when we are considering the bill. I do not see any retroactive feature in the legislation. Owing to the fact that it was not put into force four or five years ago, as it should have been, many sons and daughters of deceased veterans have already attended universities and have paid for their own courses. They have probably borrowed the money to do so or the widowed mother, the pensioner, has borrowed the money to assist them in obtaining an education. I see no provision in the bill to treat those who have already received and paid for their education in the same manner as those who will come under the act when it is brought into force this year. I wish to express this complaint now, before we deal with the various provisions of the bill.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group certainly endorse the principle of the legislation and are very pleased to see the bill introduced. I know the Legion has made proposals along this line to the government and the veterans affairs committee for a number of years. It is my recollection that the matter was first discussed, as was said by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and as the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) reminded me a few minutes ago, in the veterans affairs committee of 1946 when a number of members of the committee tried to get this type of legislation incorporated in the veterans charter.
While the government is late in bringing the legislation before the house, we are very pleased to know that at last, so far as the principle is concerned, they have responded to the pleas of the Canadian Legion. I think it is quite fair to say in that respect. that it is the good and continuous work of the Legion and the national council of veterans that has finally caused the government to give consideration to their repeated representations and recognize the principle of educational assistance to the children of deceased veterans.
In addition, the subject has been raised a good many times in the house by members particularly on the opposition side, and as far as the principle of the bill is concerned I am sure we are very pleased that the government has recognized it. However, I am not clear as to the exact meaning of one or two of the clauses, and I am sure when we get into committee a number of members will want the minister to explain the meaning of certain clauses. If I understand the bill correctly that $25 per month is the sum total, together with educational costs, then

under present day circumstances that appears to be too small an amount. But we will wait until we get into committee, and I hope the minister will be able to give us further information as to those sections which concern us having to do with the amounts payable.
Once again, we are pleased to see the government recognizing this principle, and once again I say that I am quite sure no bill affecting such a relatively small number of persons in Canada will produce more happiness than this one, particularly if the government sees fit to raise the amount payable to a satisfactory figure.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group commend the government for introducing legislation of this type, and we are fully in accord with the general principle thereof. But I was under the impression that under the legislation both the cost of the education of the dependent of the veteran and a living allowance of $25 a month would be paid. I now have some doubt in my mind whether or not the full cost of education is to be met. Therefore before I say any more I should like to get a further explanation from the minister regarding section 4	(2) particularly. I
should like to know exactly what it means, because if it does not mean that the full cost of education is going to be met then I shall not be quite so complimentary in my remarks.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks about the measure. As hon. members who have already spoken have said, for some years there has been a demand by the members of the great Canadian veterans' organizations and also by many members of the house for some legislation which would assist the children of Canadians who gave their lives for their country. It has been felt that such children were bound to be under a handicap compared with other children because of the fact that their fathers had lost their lives in one or other of the services. There has also been a feeling that these young people should be put in a position where they could take pride in the service their fathers had given, and that the service of the fathers should be recognized by some measure of assistance to the sons and daughters.
The measure does go part way to meet the suggestions that have been made, and I join with other members of the house in commending the minister and the government for the start. It took a great deal of pressure to get this far, but now we are here a word of commendation is in order. But
Armed Forces
I believe the measure will not help a very large number of such children. During the debate on the resolution the minister explained that only those who had completed their secondary education would receive any benefit, and he said in effect that only those children intending to take university training would be eligible for help. He pointed out that whereas there were 12,000 children who had lost their fathers, only about 10 per cent of them would benefit under the legislation, or approximately 1,200.
It must be evident that those who are not going to go to university will constitute the largest group of these children. They are the ones who will be entering one of the trades or some occupation which does not require a university degree. Yet these children appear to get no benefit whatever under the measure. They are left to what they can get from the regular public schools, and I think that is unfair. They get no living allowance whatever, and of course that is an important feature of the assistance given by the bill. It provides for the payment of university fees. Children who are not going to go to university of course would not have to pay fees in a technical school but their maintenance must be provided, and I suggest they should be eligible for this payment in the same way as children who are going to university.
Under the rehabilitation plan in effect for the veterans themselves, no such distinction was made. If a veteran wished to take vocational training he got his allowance just the same as a veteran who went to a university. But here we come to deal with the children of the veteran who lost his life, and under the definition only the one who goes to university can get help. I am very glad that he or she will get that help, but the one who wants to take up a vocation gets no help whatever. To me that is one of the great weaknesses in the bill.
We always understood that the assistance would be on the same basis as that given to the veterans, but the allowance is only to be $25 per month whereas the amount payable to the veteran himself was two or three times that amount. This payment of $25 per month is merely a token payment, and obviously was not intended to provide for the subsistence of the veteran's children while taking a course.
Then there is one other point I should like to draw to the attention of the house, and that is that this bill is of no help whatever to the children of the man who, at the time of his death, was in receipt of war veterans allowance; at least that will be true in most

Armed Forces
cases. These men only received war veterans allowance, at least a great majority of them, because they were front-line soldiers. The war veterans allowance is based on front-line service. I suggest that the children of these men should be made eligible for this assistance, in addition to those coming under the schedule of the Pension Act.
I hope these suggestions will be considered by the minister, and that it will be possible to have some amendments made as the bill goes through the committee. This year we should have had a committee on veterans affairs to deal with this measure and the one which has just been passed. Here we have another good example of the folly of not having a veterans affairs committee of this house. This bill will not receive the consideration from the committee of the whole house that it would have received from a special committee on veterans affairs. I hope that during the next session provision will be made for the setting up of a permanent committee on veterans affairs.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext: According to the definition, Mr. Chairman, an educational institution means a university, college or other school of higher education in Canada. During the time when the veterans themselves were attending schools, provision was made to enable them to take educational courses outside of Canada if there was not a course in Canada that suited their requirements. I wonder if that same provision will apply so far as these children are concerned?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext: The hon. member for Royal is quite right, Mr. Chairman; that principle was followed when the veterans legislation was applied. The education had to be obtained in a Canadian institution, unless it was established that the course which the veteran desired and which was necessary for his rehabilitation could not be provided in Canada. It is not felt that the same situation exists merely in providing what I may call ordinary university training for these children.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister if a university, college or other school of higher education includes vocational training schools?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext:
It will depend on the type of vocational training which is sought. The purpose of this act, as the title shows and as the explanation pointed out, is to give

assistance to those seeking a higher education, in other words, university training; or for that type of vocational training which requires a high school education as a preliminary. It has been felt, and this is the experience of the department and the people who are in the educational spheres in this country, that that is the type of education which is most costly and which is most difficult to obtain because of financial reasons.
If the type of vocational training desired is one which can be provided by the provincial institutions which exist throughout this country, and does not call for a high school education as a requirement for entering the course, then the provisions of this bill will not be applicable. If it is vocational training such as nursing, which I mentioned before, or other types of technical training which I understand call for high school education, then the provisions of this bill would apply. In other words, I might say that the criterion is the need for a high school education as the requirement for entering the course.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext:
I certainly am not in agreement with that definition. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra pointed out, there will not be many who will benefit by this bill. Since the end of the last war the whole emphasis has been on university training. Practically all of the government assistance has gone in that direction. Today you can go to the employment offices across this country and find queues of unemployed who have no training of any kind. At the same time you will find vacancies listed calling for skilled tradesmen such as bricklayers, pipe fitters, carpenters and glass fitters. I am afraid that if we continue this type of assistance in the field of education, in a few years there will be no hewers of wood and drawers of water but everyone will be running around with a university education and not producing very much.
I feel that the minister would be well advised to consider including vocational training schools in this definition. For example, a young girl taking a commercial course which requires a year or eighteen months of study in a local school would receive no help. There are many of these schools across the country, and some of them are costly. There is transportation involved. According to the definition in this bill, such a girl would not be eligible for assistance because she is not attending a recognized university but is merely attending a school which teaches a commercial course.
The time to iron out these definitions is now, and not by correspondence after the bill has passed. There are these vocational training schools across this country in which

young men do not get a high school education, but they receive a basic education which is sufficient to enable them to take a course in the trades.
In many cases the people who require the assistance most are those who cannot afford to send their children through high school but have to take them out in the ninth or tenth grade and send them to a vocational training school because they cannot afford to put them through high school and thus give them university entrance. If the government is desirous of helping the largest group of veterans, in my judgment they should include vocational training schools in this type of assistance. If they do not do that, I think most of the assistance will be going to people who could perhaps afford to send their children through; because if you can get them through the university entrance, you are not badly off. But as to the great majority of the ex-service personnel who will raise a family and try to educate them, the vocational training school is the spot, in my opinion, where we should try to give them the greatest assistance.
As I pointed out before, the lack of trained tradesmen in this country is terrific. The whole emphasis of the Department of Labour in immigration has been to bring skilled tradesmen from Europe. The importation of stenographers right here to this city from Great Britain only a few months ago is an indication that a great deal of assistance is necessary in relation to this type of work. There are thousands of girls running around the streets and standing behind counters for low wages because their parents could not afford to put them through the commercial course that would enable them to take such a job. I believe the thinking of the government in the field of education must be focused on the need for training in these skilled trades in this, country rather than depending on immigration as we have been doing since 1945. This would be a good place to start, by including vocational training schools in the definition under section 2 of this act.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I must agree with many of the things that have been said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. This whole system of education, as we are seeing it develop across the length and breadth of Canada, it seems to me is creating a number of square pegs to be fitted into round holes. Those who returned from the first world war know that the assistance in the matter of education was completely and utterly inadequate. Those who returned from world war I certainly had to make their own decision as to what line of education they were going to take up, and rightly or wrongly
Armed Forces
they pursued what they considered to be the type of training they were to follow.
The day is going to come, it seems to me, when we shall find this situation if we continue the type of education that is mentioned here in the bill-not that I am particularly opposed to it, except that I think it should be broadened. For instance, today in the great Kitimat development in British Columbia we have dishwashers on the job who are earning more than are university graduates. That is a fact. The reason they are earning more is certainly not that they are more skilled but rather that they are willing to take on a type of work that is not particularly edifying. All through the industrial set-up of the Dominion of Canada, as we continue to prosper and develop, we are going to find increasing numbers of instances similar to that which you find today in this developmental work at Kitimat.
Further than that, if the children of civilian residents of Canada are going to pursue university courses and the veterans' children are going to be subsidized by governmental action to do likewise, then the day is not going to be too far distant when most of the so-called workers of this country are going to be working for the government. It seems to me that the idea behind any legislation of this type should be that we are building up the boys and girls of today who are going to be the men and women of tomorrow, and who are going to be producers for the economic development of the Dominion of Canada.
Rightly or wrongly, we may be critical of university graduates but the fact still remains that the real basic principle upon which our development depends is not in having men and women who have possibly a greater than technical school education, but in having men and women who are ready and willing to throw themselves into the economic development of this country. For a long time I have been of the opinion that we have been stressing the university too much and neglecting our secondary and trades schools all across Canada. In my opinion they are the institutions that will turn out the real men and women for the development of this country in the future.
I have to go along with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Cape Breton South in pointing out these facts. For our future economic development, in my opinion it is necessary that consideration should be given to the interpretation of this bill that is now before us; not that by any manner of means we should exclude university graduates, but we certainly ought

to have a complete definition of the type of person this legislation is going to benefit. When it comes to children in an orphaned family, I certainly do not think the higher university education is going to be particularly applicable, because a university education today costs a great deal of money and it certainly takes the head of the family all his time in toil, tears and sweat to earn sufficient to put a boy or girl through university. Where the head of the family has been removed, the onus of responsibility will fall upon the remaining parent. I feel strongly that this type of definition as to beneficiaries under this act should now be explicit.
As far as schools are concerned, I believe the trade schools and the vocational training schools are the real schools that are going to build boys and girls into men and women of tomorrow for their purposeful tasks in developing and increasing the economic advantages of this country of ours.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS

Certainly I think at the present time there is a much more acute shortage of people with commercial training and trades training than there is in some of the more learned professions. There are two specific questions I should like to ask the minister. I should like the minister to clear up that point. A second group of people whom I have wondered about were those taking accountancy. In most instances students taking accountancy do not actually attend a university. [Mr. MacDougall.l

speechtext: I should like to comment on this without delving too deeply into the merits of this or the other kind of education. Why should we pick out some of them and educate those who are taking this type of education mentioned here, and say we will not educate the others? I can see no argument in favour of that at all.
