subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext:
I think the resolutions passed by the Canadian Legion indicate very clearly what a great weakness it is in the bill that no provision is made for vocational training. I hold in my hand two resolutions which were passed at the dominion convention of the Legion last year on this point. One was in these words:
Resolved that all such entitlements and credits, etc., which the veteran would have received had he been spared to return be made available to his family.
The other was more specific. It read as follows:
Be it resolved that the federal government be requested to instigate a policy for the children of deceased service men similar to that in force for single student veterans attending university or vocational training schools and receiving a monthly allowance under the rehabilitation act.
When the Legion came before the cabinet in November of last year they had this recommendation to make on the point:
Recommendation-in respect of children of deceased service men
That the federal government instigate a policy for the children of deceased service men similar to that in force for single student veterans attending university or vocational training schools and receiving a monthly allowance under the rehabilitation act.
Therefore it is perfectly clear that the Legion had in mind benefiting the whole range of children of deceased veterans; and we all know that the great majority of these children would be more apt to benefit from vocational training than they would university training. The minister himself said on second reading

of the bill on April 13 that only 10 per cent of the 12,000 would get any help under this measure. In effect what he is doing is giving the green light to the children who propose to take university training, and putting up a red light against the other children who would like to get vocational training.
He explained on page 3754 of Hansard what type of training would be covered when he said, in addition to the university:
Teacher training, through the provincial normal schools, and nursing, through the teaching hospitals, are cases in point.
But he has not given the house or the committee one example of assistance in vocational training, and there is where the great need exists. With regard to vocational training he takes the position that any of these young people who want to get vocational training can get it in the provincial schools that are already set up. That may be true in so far as paying fees is concerned; they may not have to pay any fees for their vocational training, but they will have to have someone pay for their subsistence while they are attending those vocational schools. If the assistance provided by this act is not extended to cover them, then I am afraid the result will be that many of these young men and women will not get vocational training at all. They will simply be cut off.
I would urge that the definition of an educational institution be broadened to include commercial and vocational training schools, just as was done in the case of the veterans of the second world war. They were not put to the obligation of going to university if they wanted to get help. They could choose themselves whether they wanted university training, vocational training or commercial training, and they got help no matter which course they followed. I suggest that exactly the same provision should be made to apply in this present measure.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext:
It seems to me that the point at issue at the moment is not a debate as to the respective merits of university training on the one hand and vocational training on the other. I think we all agree as to the value of both. Certainly there is no question but that our country's life is richer because many veterans of world war II were enabled to go on and take university training. I for one am very glad to see that provision for university training is included in this bill. But we also recognize that Canada's well-being is advanced by everything that is done to increase the vocational skill of those who are not able to go on and take university training. In other words, it seems to me we are not indulging in an academic debate between those two types of training. What we are asking is that there be no discrimination
Armed Forces
between them, but rather that this assistance be available in either case.
I recognize that the Minister of Veterans Affairs may be sitting there thinking that we did not hear what he said a while ago, when he made it clear that the criterion would be whether or not the student had been through high school. I heard that, and I can see what might be involved in lowering that criterion; but this question presented itself to me. What about the student, be he interested in university training or in vocational training, who is unable to get through high school? Is not there a case for assistance in some instances at that level?
The minister may say that in most provinces of the country high school education is free, at least so far as tuition is concerned. But the financial circumstances in the home may, in many instances, prevent young people from getting to high school, whereas with a little assistance they might be able to do so. On the ground that the country is richer, both for vocational training and for university education, I think both should be included.
I think consideration should also be given to providing at least the allowance of $25 per month which would make it possible for students to get through high school who otherwise would not be able to get through. That would at least put them in the position of being able to go on with their university training or their vocational training.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext: I understood it was not so much a question of whether or not a young person had gone through high school but rather whether, the young person having gone through high school and then applying for vocational training, such type of training would require that the applicant had gone to high school. That is the difference. It seems to me that if the young person prefers that type of vocational training which does not require high school, then at least some allowance for the cost of living could be made. I should think that $25 a month might well be allowed, even though there would be no cost of education involved.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra is right in pointing out the definition of an educational institution where reference is made to a university, college or other school of higher education in Canada, as approved by the minister. Of course the expression "higher education" is elastic, and the minister can define that so as to include technical schools and the like. But I think he will agree that ordinarily higher education would not include trade schools.
The minister did make the point at the outset that this grant was payable only to those

Armed Forces
who had graduated from high schools, or had equivalent status. I must say I have some considerable sympathy for that. The hon. member for Cape Breton South made reference to secretarial schools and business schools, and suggested that the grant should be made to assist persons going through those schools. My thought in the matter is that before they go on to business schools they should first go through high school, learn how to spell and be able to take a letter reasonably well. Many of them cannot do that.
I doubt whether this grant should be made available as has been suggested. Certainly in every province of Canada, and I think in almost every centre, high school education is available. It may be that in some instances the students would have to live with relatives, or something of that kind, but we do have consolidated schools as well as big high schools in our cities and towns. I should think those children should first of all go through high school. Then, having done that, this assistance should be made available to them if they wish to go to a secretarial or to a trade school. We have such places in Halifax. I think there is some confusion in the minds of hon. members as to whether they have to go through high school first.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS

I do not wish to disagree with one of my colleagues, but I cannot agree with the last speaker because I have had far too much experience in this particular field. I know that many of these boys and girls simply drop out of school as soon as they are permitted to do so, perhaps at about 16 years of age, in order that they may contribute to the family budget.
I could not be more heartily in accord with anything than with some remarks made this afternoon suggesting that in this bill there should be provision for vocational and technical training. I believe it was about two years ago that I received a summary from the employment service in Hamilton showing the number of women available for employment. Most of them were seeking work which did not require any particular training. It appeared from the breakdown that out of some 90 about 8 or 9 were quite capable of taking commercial training, but they had been unable to do so because of financial circumstances.
I do not think there is a centre in Canada today that is not short of stenographers. There is a great need for and shortage of them. I firmly believe that some provision should be made in the bill because, from the
[Mr. Nowlan.l
experience I have had and the instances which have come to my attention, I am sure that many of these young people who could benefit by vocational training are going to drop out of school at the age of 16, or whatever age their school system permits. subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I agree with most hon. members who have spoken this afternoon. I am sure it was the intention of the Legion and others that all should be treated as nearly alike as possible. We recall that the returned men who could not take the educational facilities offered were given the advantages of the Veterans Land Act, or some other advantage.
One hon. member has said that this is discriminatory legislation. If a boy wants to be a carpenter or a girl would like to be a stenographer, then it seems to me that he or she should be given the same opportunity as the boy who wants to be a lawyer. Some provision should be made in the measure to provide that this boy or girl shall have his or her opportunity, just the same as the boy or girl who may wish to become a lawyer or doctor.
I do not agree that there are too many college graduates in this country. We all know there is a scarcity of doctors and engineers as well as those in other professions. There is also a great scarcity of people who are technically trained. I would hope that the minister might see his way clear to amend the measure so as to give us a more comprehensive definition of what an educational institution might be, and that in so doing he would include technical and vocational education.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext:
I appreciate the debate that has taken place and the suggestions made by hon. members. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggest that the debate should not degenerate into one in which the relative values of university and vocational training would be set out. That is not the purpose.
This is something completely new in the way of veterans' legislation. Representations have been made to us upon various occasions and have been discussed at various times with people who are interested in the subject. It was pointed out that secondary high school, technical and commercial education in most cases could be obtained in provincial-controlled institutions throughout the country. It was said, however, that assistance should be given to the son or daughter of a widow, or to an orphan who would go to university

if the financial means were available to do so. It was urged that similar assistance should be given to those wishing to enter various other professions which do not call for university training, but training for which would require a high school education as a preliminary.
We looked into all the kinds of assistance that could be given, and as a result this plan was evolved. I think it is incorrect to say that it represents discrimination. As I pointed out before, the bill is designed to assist the children of deceased veterans to obtain a higher education. That does not mean that vocational training is not necessary in the economy of the nation. I think this bill marks a step forward in veterans' legislation. Hon. members can look at veterans' legislation anywhere else in the world, and they will find that this is the first legislation of this type introduced in any parliament.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR HIGHER EDUCATION OF CHILDREN OF CERTAIN DECEASED MEMBERS
speechtext: Let us make it good.

There is no doubt in my mind that the legislation is discriminatory. It does not meet the demands made by the Legion at their last convention. The ordinary person who does the necessary work of this country to produce our wealth does not need French, Latin, geometry or a knowledge of economics that he would get in grades 11 and 12. Those papers dealt with the new economics that came out of this war, the changes in currency and all that kind of thing. That is an angle that must be taken into consideration, the small percentage of the pupils who are able to go right through the different grades and graduate. There is a very high percentage who cannot do that.
There is a great waste in education when no aptitude tests are given to determine just exactly what a boy or girl may be fitted for. This legislation closes the door to vocational training schools. I am sure if the officials of the Department of Labour were asked their opinions they would tell you in no uncertain terms that the great need in this country is for skilled workmen. Many of our provinces, particularly the maritime provinces, are having an awful job maintaining or establishing vocational training schools in sections where they are badly needed.
There is an obvious situation that exists in all the industrial sections of this country, as is indicated by the vacancies for skilled workmen in all the employment offices. Some hon. members seem to be of the opinion that if they do not get through high school they can walk out on the street and find jobs. What kind of jobs can they take? The employer in the building trades wants trained carpenters, bricklayers and lathmen because they are not so apt to waste materials.
If the policy of the government is that everyone in Canada is going to have a diploma, is going to be an economist, a chartered accountant or something like that, and we are going to draw from Europe by way of immigration our tradesmen and general labourers, that is fine. university? Those children are going to end up as the displaced persons in a program of this kind.
I am not going to argue this any longer, as I have been arguing it since 1940. Apparently we are not making very much progress. speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 332, respecting the Canadian forces.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before we give second reading to this bill I think the minister should perhaps make a statement in connection with it.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is an amending bill. It amends two statutes and a set of regulations affecting service personnel. In speaking to the resolution on April 2, as reported at pages 3550, 3551 and 3552 of Hansard the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) generally reviewed the contents of the bill which was later presented to the house. I think he covered all the salient points in the bill. The sections of the bill are not all related to each other nor to one specific matter. It would probably be more helpful to hon. members- or at least I hope so-if we were to go into committee and I were to explain the various sections as we come to them.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I find it extremely difficult myself to speak on second reading as far as this bill is concerned because the only principle I can see in it is the principle of amending the Canadian Forces Act. There are at least four distinct matters involved. One makes it possible for Canadian military courts to try offenders against the laws of the country in which a military force happens to be stationed. The transfer of custody of offenders is the second one. So far as the first of these is concerned, the general principle is one that probably everybody in the house would be agreeable to, namely that Canadian courts should have the power to try Canadian personnel serving in Korea, Germany, Japan or wherever it may be. In regard to that and in regard to this matter of transferring offenders from civil custody to military custody there are several points which do not, on first reading at least, appear to one as being entirely reasonable, and some of these require a fuller explanation.
As I see it, one regulation in particular makes it possible for a soldier who has been found guilty on two or more counts-although the conviction on one of these counts may be quashed by a higher authority, or by an

appeal, or by anything else along that line and therefore the sentence which is awarded is quashed also-to receive whatever sentence the army authorities deem reasonable for the charge which was not quashed. Under that provision it is made possible for the soldier to be awarded a heavier sentence for the one charge that is not quashed than he received for the two or three offences for which he was sentenced in the beginning. That does not seem quite a reasonable proposition. Perhaps the minister will have some explanation for that particular matter.
Then the Defence Services Pension Act is also a matter which is quite technical, and perhaps it is no use to say anything about it at this moment.
The fourth matter dealt with is the voting _ regulations for the Canadian services. In connection with this I hope the minister will be prepared to tell us, when we get into committee, how the lists of service voters are to be prepared; whether they will be available; how the candidates can secure lists of the service voters who will be voting in their particular constituencies, and to what extent national defence headquarters and command headquarters will be required to co-operate in providing these lists. I trust he will deal with questions of that nature.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The
last speaker has said that several specific matters of legislation are included in this one bill, and it is pretty hard to discuss the underlying principle affecting it because there are at least four underlying principles contained therein.
A moment ago the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) referred to the voting regulations and asked certain questions with respect to them. I am glad to see that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) is in the house, because I am quite sure he will have to reply to the last speaker that if this bill passes in the form in which it now is it will be impossible to answer any of these questions, since no one can tell what will be done in that situation.
There is a matter of principle here, Mr. Speaker, to which some reference should be made. Some time ago this house appointed a special elections committee, which gave a great deal of detailed consideration to the revision of the elections act. I am not sure how many times that committee was organized before I became a member of it in 1951. If my recollection is correct, that committee sat in 1950, and in other years. However, it did not complete its work to the extent that it could report. In 1951 the
Canadian Forces Act
committee sat for many, many weeks. We had numerous sessions. The evidence was printed. I think hon. members will agree that the committee worked reasonably hard. Among other things we considered were the defence voting regulations. Finally we achieved a unanimous report, recommending a certain procedure which should be carried out. For the first time it was thought we had the basis whereby the candidates who might be involved in an election, the service personnel who were voting and the government which was responsible might all feel there was some reasonable hope of the matter being worked out satisfactorily and well. The report came into the house and was accepted, and finally legislation was passed which was based on the committee's report.
I suggest that when you look at the regulations, when they are before us in committee, you will find that all the work which was done by this committee has been scrapped, and we are back again somewhere below the surface. It is hard to understand what has taken place. We had provided for certain forms, for instance, that should be completed. We regularized the matter in two different ways. In the first place, provision was made for those who were then in the armed forces-that was 1951-to complete certain forms within three months after the act came into force. That was form 50. We also went further and said that once a year every year thereafter they would change the form. That was to provide a revolving situation so they could adjust to changing circumstances. Then we had another form for those who came in after that date.
Therefore the mechanism was set up so that the whole matter was put on an orderly basis in 1951, and from then on presumably it would work in that way. If the department carried out its responsibility under that act, one would assume there would be no necessity for changing the act now; but as the matter stands-and this will appear in the committee when we come to the bill-we will find that all these things have been changed. Instead of this work being done in 1951, as it was supposed to have been done, it now can be done up to the date of dissolution, whenever that may be, and if it is not done by then it will be done up to the election date.
I do suggest, Mr. Speaker, that a principle is involved there, in so far as legislation which was considered as carefully as this was, which we now find to be virtually repealed and scrapped, and which is to be dealt with in the house now when we are almost within the shadow of prorogation. Some very definite

Canadian Forces Act
explanation must be given of that. I think it is not a principle which this house should accept nonchalantly. All of that work should be not scrapped without more of an explanation than the very casual one that was given here this afternoon. I do not want to go into detail on this now, because it is a subject that can be dealt with in committee.
I would ask you to call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Offences out of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
This section uses the following language:
An act or omission that takes place out of Canada and would, under the law applicable in the place where the act or omission occurred-
That is, the country in which our troops were stationed.
-be an offence if committed by a person subject to that law, is an offence under this part, and every person who is found guilty thereof is liable to suffer punishment as provided in subsection two.
Is there any loophole or provision whereby that which might not be an offence in Canada, but would be in a country in which our troops were stationed, would not be looked upon as an offence if committed by one of our troops stationed there? I am thinking particularly of liquor laws and things of that kind, which constitute a problem in every province of Canada because the laws differ from province to province. Let us consider particularly troops of ours who might be stationed in a Mohammedan country where liquor is not allowed. What provision is there to cover a situation of that kind?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, under the circumstances outlined by the hon. member we would not have to prosecute. This section is in the interests of our own troops in Europe and other countries so that, by the enactment proposed herein, we may make the laws of another country part of the law which we can administer. We do this by giving our service tribunals authority to deal with offences committed by our service personnel against that law rather than have such
[Mr. Nowlan.l
offences dealt with by the criminal courts of that country.
This becomes important because in our treaty with West Germany, in our NATO treaties and in countries such as Japan where, as yet, we have no arrangement in this connection, the section gives us jurisdiction pursuant to which we could deal with these matters. I understand that under the West German treaty we will be required to administer the law of that country in accordance with its tenor. Under the NATO agreements, if it is an offence under our law we have concurrent jurisdiction. In other countries we have the right to negotiate, the idea being that we take all possible power to handle in our own military tribunals all .offences which may occur by reason of the activities of our forces in those countries.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am in full agreement with our having power to deal with such offences in our own military courts. I believe that is an extremely important move. The only point that concerns me is something which might be considered an offence in another country, one in which our troops might be stationed, but which would not be an offence in this country and subject to punishment. I am thinking particularly of sumptuary laws, and things of that kind. In other countries there are laws which we would consider quite peculiar. It would seem to me unreasonable that a soldier serving abroad and living in the way he was accustomed to live in Canada, but breaking a sumptuary or other law which would not apply here, should be subject to military discipline under this section.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: If military personnel are to be dealt with on the basis of offences under the law of the receiving country, then it seems to me it is better for us to have power to deal with them ourselves. Otherwise that country would have power to deal with them, and might regard such offences far more seriously than we do. We would deal with the situation in the light of our own legal background.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I would agree with the minister so far as that is concerned, that it is much better for us to have power to deal with them ourselves. I think there is no argument on that point. My only thought was that we might have an amendment whereby a man who broke a law such as I have mentioned in a foreign country, but had committed an act which would not be considered contrary to law in this country, would not as a result be liable to military punishment.

In subsection 2 it says that where a service tribunal finds a person guilty of one of these offences-
-the service tribunal shall impose the punishment in the scale of punishments that it considers appropriate, having regard to the punishment prescribed by the law applicable in the place where the act or omission occurred and the punishment prescribed for the same or a similar offence in this act.
And the explanatory note say this:
This is necessary 'because foreign law in some cases makes provision for types of punishment unknown to Canadian law.
I think there is another basic objection to subsection 2, in that the scale of punishment is not definitely set down. The scale of punishment laid down here will be what the tribunal considers appropriate. In other words it places much greater power in the hands of a military tribunal than resides in an ordinary court of law under any other circumstances; because a judge or jury, or whatever the case may be, in an ordinary court of law, or a court martial in respect of a military tribunal, can impose only those punishments which are definitely laid down. In this case the military tribunal is put in the position where it decides what the scale of punishment shall be. That is a basic weakness, and the sort of thing which should be avoided if at all possible.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Perhaps I should point out that, as provided in subsection 4, any offence that is within the code of service discipline, and also against the law of the country in which the troops are stationed, can still be tried under the code of service discipline.
Replying to	the	hon. member,	I wouldpoint out that in my view where subsection 2 refers to a punishment which a service tribunal considers appropriate, having regard to the punishment	prescribed by	the	lawapplicable in the country in which the troops are located, it means that our service tribunals would	take	cognizance of	the	lawsapplicable in	our	own country	to	such
offences as well as in the country where the offence was committed. It does not say that our military tribunals must apply the penalties which would be applicable to people within that country who committed these offences; it is the penalty which the tribunal considers appropriate, having regard to all the circumstances. When you are dealing with offences under the laws of another country which are foreign to our laws, I do not think you can very well set out a scale of punishment. I think it must be left to the service tribunal. The point is that we have endeavoured to give as wide a jurisdiction as possible to our service tribunals.
Canadian Forces Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I can understand the difficulty of laying down a definite scale of punishments, but I would think this section would be much safer if an addition was made to the last phrase. This reads:
-the punishment prescribed for the same or a similar offence in this act, the Criminal Code or any other act of the parliament of Canada.
I suggest that the words "not greater than" should be added before that phrase. As it stands now, the scale of punishment is entirely in the hands of the tribunal. What tribunal A might think appropriate might be only half as much or might be twice or three times what tribunal B might think was appropriate. In other words you are going to have a great deal of variation if you leave it in the hands of the particular tribunal.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
May I point out that in this section we are dealing with offences which are not offences under our laws; they are offences only under the laws of the country where the troops are located. I do not see how we can apply an exactly parallel construction to that obtaining in our own Criminal Code.
I might observe that in any event the punishment meted out by the service tribunal under this section would be subject to review the same as any other sentence.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not quite follow the minister when he says that this is for offences which would not be offences in Canada. If that is so, why put in the words "punishment prescribed for the same or a similar offence in this act, the Criminal Code or any other act of the parliament of Canada"? Those words make it quite definite that what is envisaged here is the meting out of punishment which will be similar to the punishment prescribed by the Criminal Code, or any other act of the parliament of Canada.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I think those words are used simply to direct the attention of the service tribunals to our Canadian law. It is a recognition of the fact that the offences will not be similar but that some guidance may be obtained from the Criminal Code. When the offence committed is somewhat akin to that covered by the Criminal Code, the service tribunal is directed to look at it and have regard for it.
This section deals with an admittedly difficult and unusual situation. In the interests of our own service people we are trying to enact a situation which will give us as wide jurisdiction as possible. I do not think we can very well lay down anything too specific in the way of punishment for crimes committed in other countries, which may be similar to crimes in this country or quite different.

Canadian Forces Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The difficulty is obvious, but does it not leave the military tribunal in a rather impossible situation? They are going to be asked to deal with cases which may be very serious from the point of view of the country in which they are committed, and which may not be recognized as offences from the point of view of our laws. I imagine that we are desirous of maintaining good relationships with these countries; and if a tribunal should impose only a nominal sentence, the country in which the offence was committed might be extremely offended. Then in what position would the tribunal be left?
It seems to me that all sorts of pressures might be brought to bear upon the tribunal in a country where the senior officers might be trying to maintain not only good discipline but good relations with the authorities of the country. Pressures might be brought to bear on tribunals to impose sentences for that purpose out of all proportion to the seriousness of the offence in the eyes of purely domestic Canadian law. The tribunal is going to have no defence, no backing which it might have by the simple provision of maximum sentences. They would then have the opportunity to sgy, "We have tried this offence, we regard it as serious, but the maximum penalty provided in our act is so and so."
It seems to me that it would be open to all sorts of misunderstandings and the possibility of the creation of ill-will if a tribunal simply imposed a nominal sentence, or what was regarded as nominal in the eyes of the country in which the offence was committed. That country might consider that the Canadians were treating it as a joke when they regarded the offence as serious.
The tribunal should be in the position of being able to say, "We will try our soldiers", or whatever rank it may be, "for having committed this offence, but the maximum penalty provided by our act is so and so." Then the authorities of the country in which the offence was committed could not say that the tribunal was treating the matter as being merely of petty importance and just going through the motions of a trial. It seems to me that it places the tribunal in a most difficult position. It is placing what is in effect a court of law in the position of being an instrument of diplomatic relationship, and I do not think a court of law should ever be placed in that position.
The minister has the judge advocate general in front of him, and I would ask him if he does not think it possible to examine the laws of the various countries in which Canadian troops are operating and work up a scale 
of punishments for offences against the laws of those countries which are not offences against the laws of this country. Something could be worked out so the tribunals could have a guide.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is the opinion of the officials who have studied this situation that to attempt to set up any code of maximum punishments to fit the different countries in which we have or may have troops would lead to complete confusion. I think what actually will happen in the cases which come before our military tribunals under this section is that the tribunal will look at the offence in the light in which it is regarded in the country where it takes place. If there is anything in the way of a parallel crime under our Criminal Code, the tribunal can consider that; but the tribunal will have to take the responsibility, having assessed these things, of deciding what is the proper punishment to mete out in the case of a particular offence. It is not anticipated that this section will apply to too many countries, and it is felt that we cannot do more than, as it were, rely on the sense of appropriateness and fairness and understanding of the military tribunals. They will be operating outside the ordinary type of jurisdiction entirely.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: What are the provisions of the corresponding legislation in the United Kingdom and the United States whose forces are also in large numbers in countries other than their own?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am informed that so far as we know neither of the jurisdictions to which the hon. member refers has formulated laws in this particular.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Why do we hasten to expose our soldiers to the possibility of being tried for offences in foreign countries which are not offences against Canadian law if neither the United States nor Great Britain has done so?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: The reason we are taking this step is to hasten to provide, as far as we can, that the substantial number of troops which we have abroad are not tried for offences by foreign courts but by our own tribunals. This section, as far as we are able to make it, is entirely in the interests of our military personnel.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Does the minister say that United States troops and British troops are now tried by civilian courts in -the foreign countries in which they may operate? Take the case of Germany, where all three countries have troops operating.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: As to Germany, I understand that United States and British military personnel still come under the terms of the occupation. They are not in the same position at all that we are. So far as Japan is concerned, without dwelling on it too much I understand that since the Japanese treaty was ratified the Americans have been experiencing a good many difficulties. We have tried in Japan, and so far have succeeded, in avoiding jurisdictional difficulties. As we are going to be asked to approve treaties to enforce the laws of the countries where our troops are stationed in respect of offences against their own laws, we feel that we ought to be in a position to do that. All this section does is put us in that position. Otherwise we have no jurisdiction at all. This provision puts us in a position where, to the extent that we can under our treaties or by arrangement or in any other way secure jurisdiction, we will be in a position to assume that jurisdiction.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Then I take it from what the minister says that neither United States nor British troops are liable to be charged with offences against German law, and Canadian troops are.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: They are not subject to German law now, but I think we are the first nation that has not had any proper arrangements to meet the situation, which will shortly arise.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh, now, now.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: What brilliance.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I understand that at present we are under the same regulations as the British and Americans and have the same rights; but that will probably end for all of us soon and we want to be in a position to protect our troops to the maximum possible for us to do so when the situation changes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: What are these other two countries doing about it?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not know that I want to develop what they are doing about it. We are trying to look after our own interests.

speechtext:
I am not going to argue points of law with a Rhodes scholar, but having read the section and the explanatory notes it
Canadian Forces Act
is my opinion that it does just the reverse of what the hon. member is arguing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: You are so often wrong that it does not worry me.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Following the hon. member's line of reasoning, if we had troops in Ethiopia and it was the law there that toenails had to be pulled out with a pair of pliers, his argument would be that we should amend our law to make it necessary to pull out toenails also.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I knew you would misunderstand. That is why I was not concerned with what you said.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: What the hon. member said was that if we had troops in another country it would look kind of bad to that country if we were rendering decisions that were not in accordance with the laws laid down in that country. That is what I understood him to say.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: The section would provide for putting our troops under Ethiopian laws, and I object to putting our troops under their laws at all. You want to have their toenails pulled out, and I don't.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is exactly what you were arguing. You may have been thinking the opposite, but I understood you to say that. An act was passed in this house in 1946, I think it was, making United States troops immune with respect to our laws. It provided that in the event such troops stationed in Canada committed an infraction of our laws they would be tried by their own tribunals and in accordance with the laws of the United States. I think this provision protects our troops who serve abroad. If they commit an act contrary to the rules and regulations as we lay them down, then they will be tried in these countries by our own tribunals, which will be guided by the wording of this section in meting out punishment. In so far as possible punishment will be as laid down in this legislation or according to the Criminal Code. With troops all over the world, I think it is good protection. I would not want to see the boys in Korea tried under Japanese law.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is what you are giving them here.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I think it is protecting them against that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: You are applying Japanese punishment.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: The explanatory notes are very clear.

Subsection 2 of the new section would authorize the Imposition of suitable punishments for such offences. This is necessary because foreign law in some cases makes provision for types of punishment unknown to Canadian law.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: That has to do with the section under discussion, and I think it protects Canadian boys serving in other countries in that they are not going to be subjected to punishment laid down by the laws of other countries. I think the hon. member for Kamloops is a bit twisted.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Would the hon. member permit me to read him the first subsection of this section; and would he also permit me, although a Rhodes scholar not claiming any special knowledge by that fact, to point out to him what is a rule of the house and of every court in Canada, namely that it does not matter what the explanatory notes say. It is what the act says that counts when you are in court, and subsection 1 of the proposed section reads as follows:
An act or omission that takes place out of Canada and would, under the law applicable in the place where the act or omission occurred, be an offence if committed by a person subject to that law, is an offence under this part, and every person who is found guilty thereof is liable to suffer punishment as provided in subsection 2.
Acts or omissions committed by Canadian troops in other countries, even though those acts or omissions are not offences against the laws of Canada, are now going to be offences under this measure if the bill becomes law, and they will be punished by an act of the Canadian parliament. Perhaps the hon. member would deal with that situation, quite apart from the fact that the explanatory note to subsection 2 deals with something which is not law but merely an explanation made by the department.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS

I have a problem that I think should be dealt with at this time. I notice that the legislation is referred to as the Canadian Forces Act. The minister will recall this particular problem because I have taken it up with him. It has to do with the navy rather than the army. In this case it was an offence committed by Canadian forces. From what information we have, it would appear that two Canadian navy boys from the ship Crusader were on leave in Hong Kong. They were arrested for being in possession of arms without a licence, and one was sentenced to 18 months while the other was sentenced to 12 months.
When I took this matter up with the minister he was good enough to make some investigation of it. He wrote me a letter
[The Chairman.]
explaining in part the difference between the two sentences, the one of 18 months and the other of 12 months. I think perhaps I should put on Hansard a clipping from the newspaper so hon. members will have the information before them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Order. Before the hon. member reads that newspaper clipping, I want to ask him in all seriousness if he thinks it is proper for him to bring individual cases to the minister's attention under this section. We are now discussing section 2 which is related to an examination of offences committed by our troops abroad. I know that the offence to which the hon. member was referring occurred in Hong Kong, but it looks as if the sentence had been passed. Here we are studying future cases. I think it would be more appropriate for the hon. member to bring up this case when the supplementary estimates of the Department of National Defence come before the committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I say to you that the clipping is not commenting on this legislation at all. It deals with an offence committed by Canadian troops in a foreign land, and that seems to me to come under this section.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I was not complaining about the clipping itself; I was just complaining about the fact that the hon. member is introducing individual cases which, apparently, have been dealt with by the court in Hong Kong, and in which sentence has been passed. Here we are dealing with a section contemplating future cases and offences committed abroad.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
What I am endeavouring to find out, Mr. Chairman, is whether or not this legislation will cover a case such as I have in mind. If it does not, then I think possibly some amendment to the legislation should be introduced now. Otherwise we are going to get into the same difficulty. The only reason I am trying to put this clipping on Hansard- I have already shown it to the associate minister-is that I was about to make some comment on the difference between the two sentences for the same offence. Then when I had read this clipping I was going to point out that while one sentence was for 18 months and the other for 12 months, the civil court in Hong Kong had reduced the 18 months sentence by 2 months. The minister explained to me that there was a mistake in the newspaper clipping, and that there had been a reduction of 2 months in the 18 months sentence. This brought the one sentence down to 16 months, while the other sentence remained at 12 months, and both sentences were for exactly the same offence.

The ridiculous aspect of the case, Mr. Chairman, is that a civil court in Hong Kong can take possession of two of our boys in the Canadian navy and impose entirely different sentences upon them for the same offence. In this particular case the lieutenant commander in charge of H.M.C.S. Crusader objected to this procedure. He used every means that was available to him to persuade the civil authorities in Hong Kong to turn these boys over to him for punishment. He could not do that because the authorities would not listen to him. We have, therefore, these two boys-particularly this one from Drumheller-serving	sentences in Hong
Kong which were imposed by a civil authority, yet apparently our own naval forces are supposed to administer justice to our own boys when they are in a foreign land.
It seems to me that, if necessary, this legislation should be amended to take care of such cases. I would ask the minister just where the justice comes in if our forces serving in a foreign port-I do not suppose you could call Hong Kong a foreign port, because it is a British possession-are subject to the jurisdiction of the foreign civil authorities and we have no say whatever over that. In my judgment the two sentences have no relation to the crime at all. Surely our government here should do something about this. I know the minister is concerned about it. He told me there were some doubts in his own mind as to just how much power the Hong Kong civil authorities had to deal with our forces.
I wonder if the minister would explain what has taken place in connection with that case, and what is going to be done in such cases in the future. If it is necessary to have some revision of this legislation in order to deal with such cases, then I think this is the time that should be done. Will the minister comment on that?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member discussed this case with me, and I may say that representations are being made concerning it. I do not think I gave him the impression, at least I hope I did not, that we could by unilateral action do anything about it. Jurisdiction to try these two sailors did exist in the courts in Hong Kong. This section which we are discussing goes about as far as this parliament can go to put our service personnel in a position to make arrangements with a colony such as Hong Kong with regard to the handling of our own criminal cases. Without this section we have nothing to stand on at all. We have no jurisdiction even if they handed the men over to us. This section represents a step toward meeting the 68108-261
Canadian Forces Act
situation, and there is another step provided in the next section.
By ourselves we cannot legislate a colony or another dominion out of its own criminal jurisdiction, but unless we take unto ourselves the right to deal with our own service personnel, as this section endeavours to do, we could not even ask the other colonies or dominions to give us jurisdiction.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: The minister maintains that by passing this section provision will be made to enable us to deal with these cases?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: We shall try, with the authority given, to negotiate arrangements in these cases to handle our own personnel. You cannot do it arbitrarily, but we would have under this section the jurisdiction if they will negotiate.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Has the minister any reason to feel that any foreign power will agree to this legislation we are passing? Unless they will agree to it, it seems to me it is worthless.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: As I understand it, under the arrangements which now exist with regard to Germany we will be charged with the administration of their criminal law as affecting our troops. Under the NATO status agreement I think we will have concurrent jurisdiction over our forces in that respect. In countries like Japan, where I may say we have been quite fortunate in negotiating temporary arrangements from time to time because they have been very co-operative, it will be a case of negotiating permanent arrangements. There will be, therefore, two or three different categories, but all of them rest on the basis that if we do get jurisdiction either by treaty, by mutual arrangement or by negotiation, this section enables us to carry out and exercise the jurisdiction we shall have obtained.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say he was making a further investigation concerning the case I brought before him?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS

speechtext: I read the words "service tribunal" in lines 15 and 17 of this section. I ask the minister to be kind enough to give us a definition of those two words.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I would say, Mr. Chairman, that the military tribunal would be a service tribunal as defined in the act which means a court martial or the person presiding at a summary trial such as the commanding officer, depending on where the jurisdiction rests.

speechtext:
Is there anything in the act to the effect that a service tribunal would operate only in certain definite countries, or in any particular country?

Canadian Forces Act

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: The service tribunal can, I suppose, in varying degrees-depending on treaties and so on-operate in any country where our troops are actually stationed. The extent to which it has exclusive jurisdiction is a matter of treaty or arrangement. It can actually deal with service offences of our troops that are in a country and offences outside of that within varying limits.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is there any treaty with one or several countries with regard to the recognition of such a service tribunal?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are conventions. I shall give two or three illustrations to the hon. member. There was a convention concluded with the federal republic of Germany on May 26, 1952. That will come into effect when the Bonn treaty is ratified. It provides-and this would be applicable to our service tribunal-among other things the following provision:
The members of the forces shall observe German law and the authorities of the forces shall undertake and be responsible for enforcement of German law except as otherwise provided in the present or in any future applicable convention or agreement.
That gives us jurisdiction in respect of their criminal law. The NATO status of forces agreement has a clause in it that gives each NATO country jurisdiction unless the offence is also an offence under our law. That is provided in this section. In some other countries we have a practical working arrangement, as in Japan. So the extent of our status depends on various factors.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Does Canada have such treaties with all countries, or with only a few?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: We have the one to which I have referred, namely that with Western Germany. We have one with the 14 NATO countries, and at the present time we are engaged in negotiating one with Japan. I think that is the extent of our treaty effort, as far as I know.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I will explain to the minister where I am heading. Germany is divided into two parts, East and West Germany. In virtue of the treaty to which the hon. gentleman referred, service tribunals are recognized in western Germany but nothing is mentioned with regard to eastern Germany. We have not any troops there yet. But if a Canadian soldier crosses the boundary between western and eastern Germany and is found guilty by a service tribunal of an offence under the laws of eastern Germany, then this legislation will support the legislation of eastern Germany

with whom there is no such treaty as the one which exists with western Germany. Then our Canadian soldier will be found guilty by a Russian tribunal in eastern Germany, in virtue of the laws in force in eastern Germany. That is why I suggest to the minister that he should be extremely cautious with regard to that legislation.
I am sure the department means well, but our soldiers may find that provisions like these may remind them of a double-barrelled gun. It is quite difficult to understand. If the minister cannot say that the service tribunals which can operate under this legislation should be only those of countries which have treaties with Canada, it may happen in other countries with which we have no treaties, and therefore it would be rather embarrassing for the Canadian soldier who may be there. It is true that we have no troops stationed now in eastern Germany, but it is easy for anyone to cross the border. If the one who crosses the border is a civilian he will fall under the law of eastern Germany, and the same thing will happen to the Canadian soldier who may cross the boundary on reconnaissance or otherwise. This therefore shows the minister how careful one must be in drafting legislation of this kind when international matters are concerned. It is an extremely difficult matter.
I would suggest to the minister the redrafting of that provision in order that consideration may be given to the Canadian soldier, the Canadian serviceman, who may have to appear in a country with which we have no treaty and who can be found guilty of any offence in virtue of the legislation of those foreign countries with which we have no binding treaties at the present time. We should be extremely careful about the matter. I am sure that it is enough to draw the attention of the hon. gentlemen to the difficulties that may arise from legislation like this, in order that some change may be made to clarify the legislation.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, one may take advantage of a tribunal that already exists. Military tribunals have existed for all time, from the time crusader King Louis IX of France rendered justice under the oak of Vincennes, from the time of the old warrior kings, to the time of the ordinary courts martial. A tribunal may be very useful upon one condition, namely that advantage is taken of it. What is the use of having military tribunals which decide nothing, as was the case after the notorious loss of the plans of the invasion of Normandy? I referred to that last week. Apparently the matter has not been submitted to any tribunal. What is the use of having a tribunal if offences as grave

as that are not referred to them? There was also the case of the careless officer who had left a top secret document on the upper shelf in the clothes closet of his hotel room. No one knows if he has been punished. Apparently he has not, because if he had been, just as much publicity would have been given to the punishment as was given to the reward of those who corrected that situation.
Another suggestion I make to the minister is that if tribunals are established or recognized, I hope they will be taken advantage of in due course.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Shall clause 2 carry?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is obvious from this and the preceding section that servicemen will be tried or may be tried by civil tribunals in foreign countries. I am not moving ahead too rapidly, I hope, but there is no provision in the next section for a review either of the sentence or of the evidence. All the original section says is that the punishment will be on the scale that is considered appropriate, but that is before a military tribunal; it is not before a civil tribunal. And as I said before, a serviceman can be tried before a civil tribunal and receive grave punishment for an offence that would not be regarded too seriously in Canada. In the next succeeding section there is no power of review of the sentence of a civil court. There is provision if the offence is committed in Canada, but not if it is committed in a foreign country. I suggest to the minister that there should be power of review, in all such cases, of the evidence and of the punishment before any final decision is made.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I inform the hon. member that under the section we have under consideration, the finding of any military tribunal will be subject to the same review and the same right of appeal to the court martial appeal board, as in the case of findings of military tribunals held in Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am referring to civil courts in foreign countries. I think they should be subject to appeal.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am beginning to be a little sorry that I ever started this argument. It seems to me that it is a very dangerous thing for us to incorporate in a section here in the Canadian Forces Act what actually constitutes a contradiction of our ordinary concept of how justice should be carried on. It places in the hands of a court not only the ordinary powers which should always reside in a court, of determining whether a crime has been committed and then imposing the sentence which is laid down by the law, but in this instance it also gives to a military 68108-261J
Canadian Forces Act
tribunal a legislative power. That is what it amounts to. It has the power of legislating what the punishment for the particular crime committed will be.
It seems to me that is completely contrary to all our concepts of how justice is administered. That is the reason I took objection to it at the beginning, as the minister will remember. I say that is particularly dangerous when you are dealing with the ordinary sort of court martial which is bound to be set up as far as our forces in a foreign country are concerned. As is usual, the court martial set up will be composed of whatever officers happen to be available at the time.
Having been unfortunate enough to be a member of a very large number of courts martial myself, I know that most people who sit on them are not too well adapted to that particular position. It just happens to be one of the military duties which an officer who is present and available has thrust upon him. In these circumstances I say that these military tribunals in most cases will not be composed of members of the judge advocate general's staff or other officers with legal training. It seems to me to be a particularly dangerous principle to put in the hands of that court what you might call legislative powers as well as ordinary powers of administering justice.
I ask the minister whether, when this section was being drafted, the advice of the deputy minister of justice and of the Department of Justice was taken in regard to this particular point especially.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: The deputy minister of justice and the officials of the Department of Justice were consulted with respect to this section, as well as other sections of the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am not able to answer specifically these two questions, but the section as it stands was dealt with by the Department of Justice and approved by them. I do not know all the minutiae they considered or what their views were. I should like to say this, that in all countries abroad where we have troops we now have a deputy advocate general who sits on every court martial. He is well versed both in military and civil law. Lastly, I should like to ask the hon. member what would be the alternative to what is proposed. Would he be in favour of handing all our military personnel over to the criminal courts of these countries? Unless we take some action such as proposed that would be the only alternative.

Canadian Forces Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have already said I am not in favour of handing them over. As far as the language of this provision is going to keep these people in our own hands to deal with, I am all in favour of it. I do suggest to the minister that some words might be put before the final phrase to the effect that the punishment awarded would in no case be greater than that for the same or a similar offence under the military code, the Criminal Code or any other act of the parliament of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
While the
hon. member for Temiscouata was speaking he reminded me of what seems to be an omission from this section, and it is a very important one. The note on the side under "Part I" says:
2. Subclause (1) would add a new section 119A to the National Defence Act. Subsection (1) of the new section would make it possible for Canadian service tribunals to enforce, in respect of members of the Canadian forces, the law of foreign countries where such members are serving.
I take it that is the intention of the section, but when you read the section you find there is nothing in it about where the forces are serving at all. It says:
An act or omission that takes place out of Canada and would, under the law applicable in the place where the ^ct or omission occurred, be an offence if committed by a person subject to that law, is an offence under this part, and every person who is found guilty thereof is liable to suffer punishment as provided in subsection 2.
That does not say anything about where the person is serving. The hon. member for Temiscouata referred to eastern Germany. But suppose a member of the Canadian forces leaves his billet in West Germany and goes on a tour through Holland, Belgium, France and Italy, and commits an offence in each country. It is not in the place where he is serving. He is not in the country where our troops are serving at all. Yet the act or omission which he commits has taken place out of Canada, and under the law applicable to that place where the act or omission occurred is an offence. Therefore it is an offence against this act; that is what is intended. What you are dealing with are offences committed by troops in countries where they are actually serving. Is that not so? This bill does not cover that at all.
Then the minister said it refers to countries with which Canada has treaties. I should say that it refers to countries with which Canada has an understanding or agreement, because notwithstanding the passage of this bill I think it will be necessary to have understandings with the authorities of the countries concerned that the personnel charged are liable under this act, and will receive due punishment for the crimes committed.
[Mr. Campney.l

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: This section would give us power to exercise jurisdiction over our own military forces. So far as East Germany and other places of that category are concerned, the hon. member will understand that they would pay no attention to our legislation anyway. We have no troops there and, in any event, they would not recognize our law at all. They do not have to recognize our law, and would I am sure pay no attention to it whatsoever.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
But to put it
another way, perhaps a soldier returning from Korea will come by ship by way of Australia, New Zealand and Honolulu. The same situation would apply there. I suggest that the minister is concerned with the country in which the troops are serving. Why not say that?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I point out that what the hon. member for Calgary East has suggested is the very antithesis of the meaning of the section. When he suggests that we make the punishment similar to what the punishment would be for similar offences under our law, his suggestion of course was frankly absurd. I am sure he was not serious; because the very purpose of the section is to cover things which are not covered by our law.
I have also listened to the hon. member for Kamloops with some interest. He seems to be appalled that we are introducing new crimes into the act. Of course we are. The very purpose of the bill is to introduce a whole series of new crimes so that we have a point of negotiation with these countries, and can say, "We can try these people, because what has been committed is now a crime under our military law as well." That is the whole purpose of it; and I am sure the hon. member for Kamloops is aware of that. But I do not understand his argument when he brings that forward as a reason for not passing the section.
Then, so far as the argument of the hon. member for St. John's West is concerned, I would say it is simply a question of interpretation of the section. There have been quite a few legal minds working on it, and I would suggest that his interpretation is the wrong one.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Obviously the hon. member has been a commanding officer too long. He loves to introduce new crimes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
