Our discussion of the section has to be in general terms. Would the minister give us some specific examples? We are talking about the application of a foreign law to personnel of the Canadian forces, and talking about new types of punishment

unknown to Canadian law. That is the expression we see in the explanatory note.
The section as it now stands, if passed, would give to a service tribunal the opportunity of imposing upon Canadian citizens who happened to be in uniform in a foreign country types of punishment unknown to Canadian law. Could the minister give us some examples that were brought to his attention, or to that of members of his department, when the amendment was drafted? Would he give some examples to indicate the foreign law' which differs from Canadian law, and the types of punishment which differ from or which are unknown to Canadian law.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I did not make any statement about military tribunals operating under this particular section imposing punishments foreign to Canadian law. This section is to permit military tribunals to deal with offences under foreign law. There are many different offences under the criminal laws of different countries. In arriving at a punishment military tribunals would look at what would seem to be appropriate, having regard to our own Criminal Code and presumably to the type of offence and the punishment in the country in which it was committed. The tribunal would have to arrive at what it considered to be under all those circumstances a proper punishment. I did not say at any time that we propose to administer punishments as contained in foreign criminal codes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
What further explanation would the minister make of that part of the section which says:
-the service tribunal shall impose the punishment in the scale of punishments that it considers appropriate, having regard to the punishment prescribed by the law applicable in the place where the act or omission occurred.
And what is meant by the explanatory note where it says:
This is necessary because foreign law in some cases makes provision for types of punishment unknown to Canadian law.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
All I can say is that as I interpret the section-and I have said this two or three times-it means that our military tribunals in those cases where they can obtain jurisdiction, by the various means I have mentioned, are to mete out the punishment they consider appropriate, having regard to the Criminal Code or other acts of the parliament of Canada, so far as they can assess and apply them in regard to the offences charged under foreign law.
Punishment under such circumstances is admittedly like any other punishment, even the punishment meted out by the judges in our own criminal courts from day to day,
Canadian Forces Act
in that it is almost entirely a matter of discretion with the judge in each case. There are various opinions held by various judges. This does not change the basic principle that the judge or tribunal must assume the responsibility for the punishment meted out, All this section seeks to do is indicate to those tribunals, if one can use a general term, that there should be a Canadian type of punishment. Beyond that the tribunal, subject to review, subject to appeal and to all the other safeguards in the National Defence Act, in the first instance uses its own discretion, having regard to all the circumstances.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Why is not
the minister willing to insert in the section a clause to the effect that where Canadian troops are serving is the only place the service tribunal will have jurisdiction? It will not have jurisdiction over offences committed at points outside of where the troops are serving, or the NATO countries to which he has referred. When our troops were training in the state of Washington was there any agreement with the United States government whereby the Canadian service tribunal could try a man for an offence committed against United States law at that time?
Supposing a man were on leave from England or Germany, and committed an offence in some place such as Ireland or Sweden, outside the NATO countries; would such offences be regarded as offences against the National Defence Act of Canada and render a man liable to punishment?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: They could be, I suppose; but we would have no jurisdiction in other countries, in any event, in respect of this or any other section.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is not really an answer to the point I raised. Supposing one of our soldiers is on leave in Sweden, a country with which there is no agreement, and commits an offence against the law of that country. Under this section it becomes an offence against this act. Thus the offender is rendered liable to punishment under the act, and trial would be by a Canadian service tribunal. But there is no agreement with the Swedish government regarding that. My understanding from the sidenote is that the amending section is intended to cover an offence where our troops are serving.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
In the case of an offence committed in Sweden, we could do one of two things. We could not seek to assert jurisdiction but we could go to the Swedish government and say, "We have authority

Canadian Forces Act
under our act to try this serviceman; will you hand him over to us?" We could not willy-nilly exercise jurisdiction, but he would be no worse off if he were in our hands. I do not think any person in the services or any other civilian is going to fare any worse by being tried by his fellow Canadians than he would if he were tried by someone else.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Does not the minister feel that there should be the power of review under that section?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS

These are not civilian

speechtext:
In addition to the matter we have been talking about, this section deals with certain other matters. The provision for the transfer of offenders seems to be quite reasonable. Subsection 3 reads:
Where the court martial appeal board has set aside a finding of guilty but another finding of guilty remains, the board shall forthwith refer the proceedings to the minister, or to such other authority as he may prescribe or appoint for that purpose, who shall
(a)	affirm the punishment imposed by the court martial if the court martial could legally have imposed that punishment upon the finding of guilty that remains; or
(b)	subject to section one hundred and seventy-five, substitute for the punishment imposed by the court martial such new punishment or punishments as he considers appropriate.
Then in subsection 4 we find this:
Where an appellant has been found guilty of an offence and the court martial could on the charge have found him guilty under section one hundred and twenty of some other offence, or could have found him guilty of some other offence on any alternative charge that was laid-
There you have the position that the minister or his appointee has the power to substitute for the punishment imposed by the court martial such new punishment or punishments as he considers appropriate. A man might be tried on a certain charge and found guilty. The court martial appeal board finds that he is not guilty of that charge, but they have the power to say that he is guilty of some other charge for which he was never tried, and to award such punishment as they consider appropriate on that other charge. That is not in consonance with the ordinary methods of discharging justice.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: The sections to which the hon. member refers provide merely for the adaptation to the procedure under the Canadian Forces Act of the present procedure contained in the Criminal Code. In other words, to save a multiplicity of trials and for various other reasons these provisions were put in the Criminal Code to allow the court of appeal to vary the charge and to change the sentence. There is nothing new about this; it is simply adopting the criminal practice of our civil courts.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is not the court of appeal that varies the sentence; the sentence is varied or a new sentence is imposed by the minister or his appointee without the man being heard on that charge.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: The minister imposes the punishment, but in the other particulars it is the court martial appeal board which acts. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: That may be covered in the act itself, but it is not covered by these particular subsections.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: It does not need to be; it is in the substantive sections of the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: The minister spoke as though it were the court martial appeal board which was doing this. If the court martial appeal board had heard the appeal and imposed a different sentence than that which had been imposed by the court martial originally, I think that would be in consonance with the general way in which justice is carried on. But it is not the court martial appeal board which does that; it is the minister or somebody appointed by him. I think it would have been better to have left the power of imposing a new sentence in the hands of the court martial appeal board.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the question?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is the minister not going to make any comment about leaving the matter in the hands of the court martial appeal board?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS

That position runs through the whole chain of sequence. The last appeal with respect to the quantum of punishment is with the minister under the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: In replying to my other question the minister did not give any specific examples. I should like to ask what purpose is served by having the service tribunal, in the words of this section, have regard to the punishment prescribed by the law applicable in the place where the act or omission occurred. What purpose is served by having the service tribunal examine the types of punishment if, as the minister says, they are to apply only to the types of punishment which are applicable under this act, the Criminal Code or any other act of the parliament of Canada?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I have already given as clear an explanation as I can. I think the intent of the section is that the military tribunal trying an offence pursuant to this section is instructed by the subsection to impose such punishment as it considers appropriate. If I interpret the words correctly, that is a discretionary direction. In other words it puts the onus on the tribunal of deciding on the punishment, "having regard to the punishment prescribed by the law applicable in the place where the act or omission occurred".
In other words, the tribunal must first look at the law of the place where the offence was committed, then at the punishment prescribed for the same or similar offences if they can be found in the Criminal Code or any other act of the parliament of Canada. I think that simply means that the tribunal looks at the punishments of the country where the offence occurred, it looks at the law of Canada and at offences under the Criminal Code or similar statutes which it thinks relevant, and then imposes the punishment that it considers appropriate. I do not think I can make it any clearer.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I come back to my original question. What types of punishment might be imposed by a service tribunal, for example in Germany, France or Belgium?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: As I understand it, the provision of lists and relevant matters is covered by regulation 27 of the Canadian forces voting regulations which, as they are a schedule to the statute, I understand have the force of law. If he will refer to page 16 of the voting regulations-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That is the very difficulty with which we are faced in dealing with these regulations tonight. As I pointed out this afternoon in dealing with the principle on second reading of the bill, these matters were considered for a long time by the elections committee and certain procedures were finally agreed upon. As I understand it, these regulations have been in operation for quite a few years. They started during the war when we had troops overseas and it was proposed to give them the right to vote, which of course they should have. Regulations were drafted for that purpose. These regulations were continued, and the whole matter came up for review before the elections committee, which spent some two years in dealing with it.
The original regulations provided for service personnel filing certain statements even

Canadian Forces Act
up to the time of the election or on election day, and having filed those they could then vote. That was the declaration on the back of the envelope, and some adaptation of that was carried on for some years. When the committee met in 1950 and 1951 and dealt with the matter, by agreement of all parties represented on the committee the machinery was amended and, I think, improved. Provision was made whereby service personnel had to file a declaration within three months after the adoption of those regulations. That was done by section 23. They then filled out what was known as form 15. Another provision was made whereby those who came in after that date would fill out form 16 showing their place of origin. Another provision was made that in December of each year thereafter, and only at that time, could service personnel change their declaration as to place of residence.
Therefore you had three forms, and a regular and orderly procedure was set up whereby records could be maintained. As was suggested by the question a moment ago, you could get access to those records to find out who was entitled to vote and who was not. As the associate minister pointed out a moment ago, section 27 of the regulations is the first procedure to be set forth in the regulations whereby lists were to be prepared and records could be obtained. As provided by that section, once a candidate is nominated the machinery is not too comprehensive. First he has to be nominated; but once nominated, and after the election has been declared, the candidate or his agent may go to the unit headquarters or national defence headquarters and obtain certain information. That was the result of the work of the committee.
We have not yet been given any suggestion as to the reason for the amendments now proposed. If the regulations have been complied with, and I presume they have been because we have been told by the associate minister and the minister that the Department of National Defence is most efficient, then by three months after June of 1951 when these regulations were passed all these declarations should have been signed, and in December, 1951 and December, 1952 anybody who wished to change his place of residence would have done so. Presumably one set of those records is at national defence headquarters and the other is following the man wherever he may be posted. If an election is called tomorrow or a month from tomorrow, it will be open to any hon. member to obtain access to these records through his agent.
When you read the proposed amendment you see that for some reason it is proposed

now to scrap all that machinery and extend the time for the filing of these declarations to the date of dissolution of the present parliament. That can be found in subsection 2 which reads as follows:
Every member of the regular forces who was such a member on the twenty-first day of June, 1952, shall before the dissolution of the twenty-first parliament complete in duplicate-
Then there is a reference to form 15. Presumably they were completed two years ago or a year ago, and I think the committee is entitled to some explanation of why these records are apparently being scrapped and new records are now going to be made.
We go on to the amendment to paragraph 34 of the regulations, and we find that if these declarations are not available on election day the voter can complete a declaration at that time. The amendment reads in part as follows:
-or, if no such statement appears to have been made, he shall subscribe to a statement in form No. 16 . . .
And so on. Everyone is anxious to see machinery set up whereby every serviceman obtains the vote. There is no question about that; but it is in the interests of service personnel as well as the government and the candidates that that be done in an orderly and regular way.
Something was said a while ago by the hon. member for Calgary East about officers being detailed for court martial work who have sometimes lacked experience. I think the Associate Minister of National Defence will probably agree with me that officers detailed for the purpose of superintending the election procedure are not very senior officers. They are probably junior officers on the stations. I have heard that some of them have used the slang expression, whatever it may mean, that they were "Joe'd" for this particular task. Some non-commissioned officer will be detailed to assist them. It is now proposed to create a situation by these regulations whereby even on election day these officers can be swamped with requests to complete these declarations.
We have had a long and interminable legal argument tonight, which shows how lawyers can become involved. I am quite certain that if the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, the Associate Minister of National Defence and I were to sit down calmly in one of our offices tonight and discuss the meaning of some of these regulations, we might spend an hour and in the end we would scratch our heads and have to admit that we were quite confused. I ask you what is going to happen when junior officers, N.C.O.'s and so on are faced with the rush and hurly-burly of an election, and twenty fellows come in and want

to vote and get away on leave. How are these regulations going to be set out; and why should they be changed now?
The questions which the hon. member tor Calgary East has suggested have to be answered. There should be an explanation as to why it was necessary to change these regulations now, and why the time should be extended up to the time of dissolution. If there was no necessity for it, then we certainly will be facing a situation which I am sure none of us want, either for ourselves or for our respective parties or for the service personnel who are involved.
I would hope the minister can give us some explanation, first as to why this is proposed, and secondly I think if the time is to be extended undoubtedly there is some reason for it. If the time is extended to the date of dissolution, then that is as far as it is possible to extend it.
After all, we are not in the confidence of the government. Frankly I do not suppose the associate minister himself knows the date of dissolution as yet. I do not assume it is going to be tomorrow or the day after tomorrow or two weeks from now. There has to be some reasonable application, and surely a provision can be made which can be followed. There could be a provision passed by this house that a declaration should be made before a certain date. After that you could get a list of the records; you would have access to the departmental records, and you would have the names and addresses of the men. There would be some order to the procedure. The matter should not be left until the election date, when there is absolutely nothing that can be done.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
There is nothing mysterious or subtle about this proposed amendment. It is an attempt to meet a situation which I should like to outline briefly. As the hon. member has just said, the voting regulations which came into effect on June 21, 1952, provided that within three months, that is by September 21, 1952, each member of the services should complete a form declaring that in the event of an election for purposes of voting his residence should be either (a) the residence of his wife or other relative; (b) the residence of himself arising out of his service; or (c) the residence he had prior to his enrolment.
Subsequently, as I understand it, those entering the service after June 1, 1952, were required to disclose on form 16 the place where they enrolled. They were limited to that place. They could not take advantage of the other two alternatives open to those who had completed form 15. Those service personnel who elected and completed form 15 68108-262
Canadian Forces Act
or form 16, as I have indicated, may in December of each year elect to change to one or the other of the three alternatives.
There has been very little trouble with respect to the last category, that is those who came into the services after June 21, 1952, because along with their attestation papers and all the other papers which they have to complete, most of them completed their declaration forms with regard to residence. But there has been a great deal of difficulty with respect to the other categories, those who entered the services prior to June 21, 1952, because they are all over the world. There have been, I think, all reasonable efforts made to get their forms completed, but the fact is, as the information has come to me, that there are about 20,000 personnel in the services who should have completed form 15 before September 21, 1952, who have not done so.
Of course that raises a problem as to whether or not these people shall be entitled to vote. The law officers of the crown, notwithstanding what may have been intended by the committee which dealt with these regulations, are of the opinion that these people who have never elected can, if they so desire, present themselves for a ballot and complete, under form 7, the declaration of their place of residence for the purpose of having their vote recorded in a certain constituency, and in that connection can select any one of the three original alternatives that were permissible in connection with form 15. If that is so it means that in certain areas where there were large numbers of service people many could present themselves in one constituency and demand to vote there. On the other hand, if the law officers of the crown are wrong, then such personnel are disfranchised; they cannot vote at all.
Unfortunately, it is probable that the adjudication of this question would not take place before an election; and whichever contention is correct, it might have the effect of invalidating quite a number of elections. For these reasons, not wanting to disfranchise such military personnel and not wanting to put them in the position where they could become the subject of agitation en masse by candidates, it has been felt that they should be given a further right of election.
I do not know how many of them will take advantage of it. There may not be any great number. However, they were serving in the forces before this procedure came into effect and it is felt that those who wish to have the right of election should have a further time to make the election which should have been made before September 21, 1952, thus declaring in what constituency

Canadian Forces Act
they want their residence fixed for the purpose of recording their vote. If they do not do that before dissolution, then along with any other people who have not taken the proper declaration they can only do one thing. They can exercise their right to vote, but they can only vote on the basis of having their vote recorded in the place from which they originally came.
In other words, on the one hand we want to prevent any activities that might lead to agitation among groups of people in places where the service people are in great numbers, and on the other hand we do not want to deprive them completely of their franchise. It is felt that the procedure proposed is fair and reasonable in both respects. That was the reason for these two amendments. It was primarily to give some further opportunity to the 20,000 servicemen who are distributed all over the world and have not so far elected. Practically all of them were in the services when these regulations were drawn, but still many of them have not complied with the regulations. Instead of just washing them out, we felt that they ought to have these two opportunities: One, to make their declaration before dissolution; or failing that, to vote if they so desired, their vote to be recorded in the constituency in which they enrolled.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That could very easily be rectified, then, without extending the time to the election date. The minister could move an amendment to these regulations to provide that those men who have not filed a declaration under (a), (b) or (c) shall be deemed to have the right to vote at their point of origin. We have their service records and we know the points from which they originated, so we would not have to wait until the election date to find out whether or not they were going to complete one of these forms. No one wants to see a man disfranchised.
I am rather surprised that the Department of Justice should say they have the right to vote anyway, despite the fact the regulations say they shall do certain things. If that is right and these men could come in and demand the right to vote, I do not see why we are passing any regulations. They had the right to vote before they filed the declaration, and if they failed to file a declaration or set forth a new declaration then they vote at the place from which they came originally.
I think if we had an amendment such as that we would be meeting the situation. But to permit the matter to go on I do not think should be allowed. After all, as to section 27 to which the associate minister referred my hon. friend, about the list and obtaining information, I think the minister will admit
TMr. Campney.]
that, under this present machinery, that is useless. It may be that all the men will file declarations. But someone has obviously fallen down on the job if over 20,000 have not filed declarations. Possibly they are not interested. We know perhaps that, as in all walks of life, some are not interested in the franchise. But it would look to me as though somebody has slipped badly is not giving these orders and not having seen that these declarations were filed. Will this give further time for the completion of these declarations and then provide that those who have not completed them can vote on election day by voting in the place from which they originally came at the time of enlistment?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
May I ask the minister what arrangements will be made for advising these
20,000	to whom he refers of this extension of time? Is it just a case of the act being passed by parliament and the news possibly getting to these men or possibly not, or can they be informed directly? If they can be informed directly, could arrangements not be made for a more definite date?
As to the suggestion that is made here, I can see the point of it, namely the date of the dissolution of parliament; but we here do not yet know what that date is although it may be that before this debate is over we shall get that information. I know that in 1949 we were informed about a week ahead as to when dissolution would be. In 1945 we were informed several weeks ahead. Mr. King talked about the efflux of time. But there have been dissolutions in history which were just like that, on the spur of the moment. If that sort of thing were to happen this time would it not be better to fix some definite date or some definite point of time and make the necessary arrangements to get that information to the 20,000 men who are affected?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The intention is, if this amendment is passed, to do two things-one, certainly. The other is still under consideration. The first is to have set out in orders to all units the course still open to those who have not complied with regulations. Second, we are also considering sending to each member of the personnel in the services a per-

sonal letter setting out the course open to him and the time within which he can take advantage of that course. We are going to make a last endeavour.
This matter has been pressed in the past but it is rather difficult to get a man to complete these forms if he is not too interested. The protection of his vote may not mean too much to him. We are intending to make a thorough final effort. How much will result from it I do not know; but we do feel that we should at least impress on service personnel the importance of the vote, because otherwise men will begin to think of their franchise only when the election approaches, and when it may be too late.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I press again the other point I was making, namely the fact that the phrase "the dissolution of parliament" does not mean much to the average serviceman. I realize that to suggest a specific date may in effect provide a shorter time, but what I am afraid of is that some of these men will confuse that phrase "dissolution of parliament" with the date of the election or the date of nomination day, or what have you. "Dissolution of parliament" is something that is known perhaps to most of the members of the House of Commons. We know what it involves and what happens. But some of these men may just put it off and decide to file the necessary form when the date of the election is announced. The time the date of the election is announced might be the very night that parliament is dissolved; and he wakes up next morning intending to attend to the matter and finds it is too late. If the minister cannot do anything else about it I suggest that in the communication to the men there should be an indication that the dissolution of parliament may happen at any time, and that they had better deal with this matter right away.

I want to support what has been said with regard to setting a definite date for the completion of these forms rather than waiting for the indefinite date of the dissolution of parliament. I am a bit surprised that 20,000 members of the armed forces have not completed these forms. From the minister's statement I gathered that there was a voluntary aspect to this thing; but the clause, as it now stands in the regulations, is mandatory. The suggested clause uses the words "shall . . . complete, in duplicate, before a commissioned officer" and so on. There is no choice in the matter. It is a military order. There must have been some breakdown in administration whereby 20,000
68108-262J
Canadian Forces Act
personnel have not completed the forms which were required to be completed. It strikes me as being a strange thing indeed.
The fact that the forces are scattered all over the world is not an impressive statement, because surely the high command is in touch with every unit, no matter where it may be. In the past the promulgation of orders has always been considered to be the only thing that was essential in order to get duties performed. The minister suggested that perhaps they might communicate with the individuals who had not yet completed the form. Again, surely that is not necessary. The commanding officers of the units, with their adjutants to do the work, are the people responsible. The publication of an order from national defence headquarters should be sufficient. But no matter how it is done, we hope it will be done quickly and that by the time the date arrives we shall not find half the number with forms not completed.
The actual date for the signing of the form I think should be set within a reasonable time; and a reasonable time for the services does not require a long period of months. This thing surely can be done quickly. Where are the man's papers? They should be in the keeping of the unit to which he belongs or at the headquarters of the formation to which he is attached. Surely the personnel who have not completed these forms can, in the usual service manner, be paraded-whether it is on pay day or on some other occasion- and these forms completed. Certainly the date should be set, I would say, within a matter of weeks and should not be extended to the indefinite time of the dissolution of parliament.

That seems to me to be just full of possibilities of all kinds of confusion. I would certainly like to know whether the suggestion of the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings has been seriously considered; that if they do not come in within the period of the delay which has been given, from that time on their votes be counted at their homes, not at their stations. If you want this latter group of people who have been delinquent in filing to vote at all, then they will have to vote where they are at their stations. I think

your point is being covered because at that time they will only be allowed to have their vote counted in the constituency in which they enrolled. They cannot elect to have it counted where they are living at the time of the election or in any other place than where they lived on enrolment. How would they actually vote in their constituencies if they are scattered all over many remote stations; how could they get to their original constituencies?

speechtext:
How do you know they are going to complete the form in this way? That is the danger when you let it go until election day. You could get a group of men in one room, and somebody would fill it out for them, as has happened before; he would fill out 20, 30 or 40 certificates and pass them out while they were smoking cigarettes. That has happened on more than one occasion. We have sworn evidence to the effect that it has happened. That was the very thing we attempted to avoid, but that is the very thing we are effecting here.
I do think there should be some further consideration given to this. The Associate Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration should put their heads together. If they did that I am quite sure they could come to a solution which would be satisfactory. In any event, there certainly ought to be some amendment to regulation 27 to give us a better opportunity to secure information than is now possible. The whole machinery that has been set up has been nullified, and I think overnight the Associate Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration should talk this over. Both these gentlemen are benign Christian gentlemen as well as the soul of honour and integrity. Since they realize the position in which they have put this house I am sure they can work together and come to a conclusion which would satisfy everybody.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS

Before we postpone this another night perhaps I might add one word. I think everybody realizes that if this amendment is carried there should not be 20,000 people on election day who will have to use form 16. We certainly hope that by the time this parliament is dissolved the number will have been materially reduced, to the point where there will be few left; and of this few, probably few will vote. But at the same time I think the committee would want those soldiers who for one reason or another, inadvertence, inability, on leave or one of a dozen
Canadian Forces Act
reasons, have not completed the declaration, assuming that they are honest men, to vote on election day somewhere, to cast their ballots in the dominion election.
Now then, the way to do that is to follow form 16, which is referred to in the section that we are dealing with. If he has not filed his declaration there, the subsection reads that he shall subscribe to a statement in form 16, and the place of ordinary residence to be declared in form 7 shall be the place of ordinary residence shown in form 16; and form 16 reads:
That my place of ordinary residence in Canada, immediately prior to the date of my enrolment, as prescribed in paragraph 23 of the Canadian forces voting regulations, was-
So and so. So we bring it down to the few people left, those who are going in on the final day to say, "On the date of my enrolment, I was living at such a place." These are the people who gave us trouble on one former occasion. I think we have a large percentage of them at this time. I am quite sure that the army, having been conscious of the difficulties which arose after the 1949 election, will do their best in the meantime to minimize it, and on election day see that it does not occur again.
